title: Can Open LLMs Generate Useful Synthetic Responses for Behavioral Experiments?
affiliations: , University of Texas at San Antonio and University of Texas at San Antonio

detail.title: Can Open LLMs Generate Useful Synthetic Responses for Behavioral Experiments?
detail.abstract: The growing use of large language models (LLMs) for synthetic response generation raises important questions about whether open LLMs can serve as viable alternatives to costly proprietary models in behavioral experiments. Using the Synthetic Experimental Data Generator (SEDG: https://synthstudy.vercel.app/), a user-friendly tool for generating persona-based synthetic responses, we evaluate open LLM performance across two studies by comparing their outputs with human-subject responses and proprietary LLM outputs. Findings suggest that open LLMs can identify the general direction of experimental effects, making them useful for theory development, pretesting, and directional validation. However, they are less reliable for precise effect-size estimation. Reasoning-oriented open LLMs perform especially well in contexts involving individual differences, though with trade-offs in speed and hardware requirements. The results also suggest that open LLM simulation works best with between-subjects designs, concise stimuli, and limited survey questions. Overall, open LLMs offer a promising, lower-cost, and privacy-preserving approach to behavioral simulation, while requiring caution in interpretation.

title: Social Media Influence and Political Party Choice among Gen Z in Ghana: Evidence from the 2024 General Elections
affiliations: , University of Ghana - University of Ghana Business School (UGBS) and University of Ghana - University of Ghana Business School (UGBS)

detail.title: Social Media Influence and Political Party Choice among Gen Z in Ghana: Evidence from the 2024 General Elections
detail.abstract: This paper examined the impact of social media on the choice of political parties Gen Z voters in Ghana will support in the 2024 general elections. The study employed the Uses and Gratification Theory and agenda-setting theory to examine four major factors behind political decision-making, including the nature of political content, trust in political parties, emotional communication, and the frequency of exposure to postings by the party. The questionnaires that we distributed among 250 university students in WhatsApp groups were used to survey students of four public universities in Greater Accra between the ages of 18 and 27. The results show that how often Gen Z sees political party content on social media is the most significant factor in which party they prefer, accounting for nearly half of their choice. The type of political content also matters, but party trust and emotional messages don't really influence how they vote. These findings go against what studies from Western countries suggest, showing that in Ghana's growing digital democracy, showing up regularly and being visible matters more than clever messages, emotional appeals, or building trust. Moreover, the findings indicate that smart Gen Z voters in Ghana base their political opinion on continuous exposure to parties on the internet instead of being structured by more thoughtful messages, unlike the traditional formation of political preferences. The research has three key contributions: it shows the ineffectiveness of Western theories on African digital democracies, where visibility often surpasses the quality of the message.

title: The Isgandarov Adaptive Transition Theory and the Isgandarov Transition Fragility Index (ITFI): Measuring Systemic Economic Vulnerability in the AI-Green Twin Transition Era

detail.abstract: The simultaneous acceleration of artificial intelligence adoption and decarbonization is reshaping national economies through interconnected structural transformations. Existing research on the twin transition largely examines these processes separately and provides limited theoretical or empirical treatment of the systemic risks arising from their interaction. This paper addresses this gap by proposing the Isgandarov Adaptive Transition Theory (IATT), which argues that systemic fragility emerges when the combined pace of AI-and climate-driven transformation exceeds the adaptive capacity of labor markets, institutions, and households. The theory is formalized through four core principles and translated into five testable propositions. Building on this framework, the study develops the Isgandarov Transition Fragility Index (ITFI), a composite indicator integrating eight dimensions of transition vulnerability, including AI disruption, decarbonization pressure, workforce adaptability, institutional flexibility, climateeconomic exposure, digital dependency, human resilience, and systemic connectivity. The index employs winsorized min-max normalization, entropy weighting with robustness checks against alternative weighting schemes, and an AI-green interaction term to capture compound transition effects. The framework is demonstrated using a fully documented synthetic panel covering 28 countries over 12 years as a methodological proof of concept. Results show that the index is computationally feasible, highly robust to weighting variation, and capable of distinguishing transition fragility across alternative scenarios. The proposed framework provides a foundation for future empirical research and offers practical applications for macroprudential supervision, sustainable finance, transition risk assessment, and adaptive economic policymaking.

detail.abstract: This research examines the structural shift from traditional search engines to generative AI interfaces, marking a fundamental transition from a referral to a destination economy. By tracing the historical evolution of search advertising-from early text ads to ambient, synthesised AI responses-the paper analyses how "native AI advertising" blurs the lines between objective expertise and paid influence. title: The Value of Credentials in Construction 2026
affiliations: , National Center for Construction Education and Research (NCCER) and Kansas State University

detail.title: The Value of Credentials in Construction 2026
detail.abstract: This mixed-methods study examined how the construction workforce perceives the value of industry-recognized credentials and how those perceptions influence career intentions, advancement, and participation in training. Conducted by the National Center for Construction Education and Research (NCCER), the study integrated survey responses from 695 eligible participants across multiple construction organizations with follow-up qualitative interviews involving 25 participants. Quantitative analyses included Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, one-sample t-tests, chi-square analyses, Fisher's exact tests, ANOVA, and ordinal logistic regression. Findings revealed that workers overwhelmingly view credentials as valuable for both hiring and promotion, with participants consistently rating credentials significantly above neutral across workforce segments. Employer support, particularly funded training, structured programs, and paid training time, was strongly associated with increased likelihood of pursuing additional credentials. While credential status alone was not significantly associated with long-term intent to remain in construction, qualitative findings suggested that credentials contribute to workers' sense of professional identity, belonging, and long-term career planning. Participants also rejected the idea that credentials function primarily as compliance tools, instead describing them as meaningful learning experiences and portable signals of competence. The findings suggest that credential systems are most effective when embedded within structured organizational support and clearly connected to advancement opportunities, workforce development, and longterm career pathways within the construction industry.

detail.abstract: This conceptual paper develops the construct of perceptual resolution to explain why practitioners operating under comparable service conditions generate different forms and levels of value. Perceptual resolution is defined as the capacity to differentiate meaningful signals within a situation, organize those signals into a relational field, anticipate how that field is likely to unfold, select leverage points for intervention, and update recognition through feedback. Drawing on practice theory, tacit knowledge, situation awareness, service research, and organizational learning, the paper positions perceptual resolution as a middle-range account of the perceptual-cognitive foundation of expert service work. The framework shows how selling, management, and learning can be understood as related expressions of a shared architecture of situated perception and judgment. It further argues that organizational learning appears not only in routines and codified knowledge, but also in changes in what practitioners notice, how they connect cues, and where they intervene. The paper concludes with implications for knowledge articulation, reflective practice, developmental design, and empirical research on expert performance.

title: When Predictive Significance Misleads Operations: Decision-and Value-Aware Inference
affiliations: University of North Carolina (UNC) at Chapel Hill - Kenan-Flagler Business School and University of North Carolina (UNC) at Chapel Hill - Operations Area

detail.title: When Predictive Significance Misleads Operations: Decision-and Value-Aware Inference
detail.abstract: Modern operations routinely turn predictions into decisions: retailers forecast demand to set prices and airlines predict bookings to manage capacity. Yet standard statistical diagnostics ask whether a feature predicts an outcome, not whether it changes the chosen action or the value it generates. This paper develops a framework for decision-and value-aware inference in predict-thenoptimize systems. We introduce two feature-level tests. Decision-aware tests ask whether a feature significantly changes the optimal action; value-aware tests ask whether it significantly changes the optimized objective. Both propagate the sampling uncertainty in the predictive model through the optimization. The resulting Wald statistics account for objective curvature, operating context, and binding constraints. Predictive, decision, and value significance can diverge because optimization changes both the effect being tested and its standard error. In simulations where we know the ground truth, the true effect of every feature on the decision and on profit, we show that the tests capture these effects correctly, including in cases where predictive testing goes wrong. We then apply the tests to a real decision on grocery scanner data: a retailer allocating limited freezer space across products. Every feature predicts demand, yet whether it significantly moves the allocation or the profit depends on the operating context and the estimation window. Our framework tells firms which features are worth acting on, monitoring, and measuring with care, and which only forecast demand, a distinction no predictive p-value can draw.

title: The Role of Digital Marketing in Strengthening Rural Enterprises: A Comparative Analysis of the Western Balkans
affiliations: University Union Nikola Tesla and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Role of Digital Marketing in Strengthening Rural Enterprises: A Comparative Analysis of the Western Balkans
detail.abstract: Aim: This paper explores the impact of digital marketing on the business performance and market integration of rural households and enterprises in the Western Balkan countries, with focus on the application of digital tools and strategies to increase market participation and visibility of rural products and services. Material and Methods: A mixed-method approach was employed, combining a systematic review of relevant literature with an empirical analysis based on data collected through an online survey of 307 rural households from Serbia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Montenegro. The statistical analysis included descriptive, correlation, and regression analyses of digital marketing and enterprise-level rural performance variables, as well as cluster analysis of the observed countries in terms of the level of digital marketing tool adoption. Additionally, the study examined differences in key variables based on whether participants had received digital marketing training. Results: The findings indicate that digital marketing-particularly the use of social media, websites, and e-commerce-shows positive associations with enhancing market participation and visibility of rural households. However, notable regional disparities persist, highlighting the need for tailored policies and increased investments in digital infrastructure and education. Conclusions: Digital transformation has the potential to support rural enterprises in achieving sustainable business practices and market competitiveness. Successful implementation requires contextspecific strategies that account for local conditions and challenges, along with ongoing institutional support and investments in building digital capacities, supported by institutional measures and continuous training in digital marketing.

title: Ability, Credit Constraints, and the Observed Returns to Child Work
affiliations: Pennsylvania State University - University Park

detail.title: Ability, Credit Constraints, and the Observed Returns to Child Work
detail.abstract: Empirical estimates of the relationship between childhood work and later human-capital and economic outcomes span negative, null, and positive values. This paper shows that a model in which the marginal human-capital effect of child work is negative at every household optimum generates the entire range. Two channels govern ability selection into child work. Without credit frictions, more able children work more only if child-work productivity is sufficiently more ability-elastic than schooling. Under a binding borrowing limit — in the benchmark without an ability gradient in child wages — more able children work more whenever the elasticity of intertemporal substitution is below one, as most estimates suggest: households that cannot borrow against a child’s future earnings raise current consumption through child work. The coefficient from regressing adult outcomes on child work then decomposes exactly into a negative displacement term and a selection term whose sign tracks the composition of ability versus wealth heterogeneity, so a uniformly negative causal margin is consistent with every observed sign. In a positive-selection economy, a credit expansion that cuts child work by three quarters — with welfare gains concentrated among the poorest households — drives the naive coefficient upward : child work looks benign precisely because the policy succeeded.

title: A Report on Patagonia's Environmental, Social, and Governance Communication Strategies and Their Influence on the Company's Overall Corporate Communication Narrative

detail.title: A Report on Patagonia's Environmental, Social, and Governance Communication Strategies and Their Influence on the Company's Overall Corporate Communication Narrative
detail.abstract: This report delves into Patagonia, an American outdoor clothing retailer's distinct approach to positioning itself as a brand with sustainable values by incorporating Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) in its internal and external communication strategies and its influences on their overall corporate communication and reputation. The main findings of this report are that Patagonia, throughout the years, has been able to place a solid foundation of its brand values while integrating ESG into its communication approach through its unconventional marketing and communication tactics. The brand uses social media, websites, partnerships, leadership communication, and its advocacy for sustainability to communicate its ESG approach. Patagonia primarily uses storytelling, both textual and visual, to convey ESG messages while collaborating with diverse in-house and contributing content creators. They do not produce traditional reports on ESG; however, they have innovative ways to transparently communicate their ESG approach through leveraging their owned, earned, shared, and paid channels. The report highlights two major recommendations for Patagonia, which are to include a broader representation of diversity across social media, especially in age and racial diversity, to enhance inclusivity. The company also needs to emphasize expanding its focus beyond environmental issues and use its platform to advocate further for social and diversity issues. The brand must consider using innovative communication platforms—such as AI—to engage a broader audience, particularly attracting younger demographics and new consumers.

title: Urban Pet Owners' Preferences for Pet Retail Chains: A Case Study of Just Dogs, Kochi

detail.title: Urban Pet Owners' Preferences for Pet Retail Chains: A Case Study of Just Dogs, Kochi
detail.abstract: The pet care industry has experienced significant growth in recent years, driven by evolving consumer preferences, increased urbanization, pet adoption and pet humanization, along with the rising demand for specialized products and services. Urban pet owners, in particular, exhibit distinct purchasing behaviors with the increasing preference for structured, one-stop pet retail chains over independent local pet stores, the industry has seen a shift towards organized pet retail formats that offer a combination of pet supplies, grooming, healthcare, and other services under one roof. This study examines the key factors influencing urban pet owners' preferences for retail chains, focusing on competitive advantages, convenience, technology integration, the omnichannel experience and sustainability concerns. Through a case study of JUST DOGS, Kochi, the research aims to analyze consumer behavior and the competitive positioning of pet retail chains.

detail.abstract: Faculty engagement with Open Access (OA) publishing remains limited in Pakistani universities, particularly in provincial and resource-constrained settings. This study examines faculty awareness, perceptions and barriers related to OA publishing at the University of Peshawar, using a quantitative survey of 318 faculty members across six disciplinary faculties. Data were analyzed using independent-samples t-tests and one-way ANOVAs. Findings reveal moderately positive attitudes toward OA, with significant disparities across gender, discipline, qualification and career stage. Male faculty and STEM disciplines demonstrated higher awareness and more favorable perceptions than female faculty and Social Sciences colleagues. PhD holders showed lower OA engagement than Master's degree holders, and a U-shaped career-stage pattern emerged, with mid-career assistant professors least engaged. The study recommends coordinated, multi-level interventions, including libraryled training, institutional APC support, and the Higher Education Commission's policy mandates with targeted outreach to female faculty, mid-career academics and Social Sciences researchers.

title: From Tokens to Atoms: Physical AI, the Artificial General Engineer, and the Economics of Automating Design, Manufacturing, and R&D
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: From Tokens to Atoms: Physical AI, the Artificial General Engineer, and the Economics of Automating Design, Manufacturing, and R&D
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is crossing from bits to atoms. In November 2025, Project Prometheus-the startup co-founded and co-led by Jeff Bezos-launched with US$6.2 billion to build an "artificial general engineer" (AGE): a physical AI system intended to compress the development of complex physical products, from aerospace engines to medical devices, from ten years to one. By mid-2026 the company had raised more than US$18 billion at a US$41 billion valuation, venture capital in robotics and physical AI had reached a record US$55.8 billion in a single half-year, and robot foundation models had become one of the fastest-growing categories of AI investment. This paper builds the economics of that transition. Extending the token-economy framework of the companion paper (Guipe, 2026) from cognitive tasks to physical production, it prices every engineering task with two inputs-design, metered in tokens, and validation, metered in physical experiments: c AGE (i) = ρ(i) τ(i) p C + ν(i) p E-and derives a two-dimensional automation frontier on which the boundary of automation is set jointly by the price of intelligence and the price of experimentation. The central result is a validation cost paradox, the physical analogue of the agentic cost paradox: because generative AI multiplies candidate designs faster than laboratories, testbeds, and certification pipelines can absorb them, the total cost-and time-of delivering a validated product can rise even as design becomes nearly free, and the share of value captured by validation infrastructure approaches one. An Amdahl-type bound shows that ten-to-one cycle compression is unattainable through design automation alone: it requires sim-to-real substitution-digital twins and simulation accepted as certification evidence-together with regulatory throughput reform, which makes the binding constraint institutional as much as technological. The framework is confronted with 2023-2026 evidence: 2.2 million AI-generated crystal structures against 41 compounds synthesized by a self-driving laboratory; an AI-discovered drug that reached preclinical candidacy in 18 months yet faces unchanged clinical trials. For the future of work, exposure inverts: the engineering professions that automated everyone else become the most exposed occupations, while Moravec-protected skilled trades-the hands that build and operate validation capacity-gain scarcity value.

title: Verification-Native Trust Infrastructure for India's Residential Real Estate Markets
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Verification-Native Trust Infrastructure for India's Residential Real Estate Markets
detail.abstract: India’s residential rental market, estimated at ₹3.6 lakh crore a year, continues to face major inefficiencies, mostly because of information asymmetry. Things like information asymmetry really show up in practice, for example, misrepresented listings and then the whole transaction process feels fragmented, almost everywhere. In this paper, the issues are looked at using information economics plus platform theory, which is a natural combination. We then lay out a verification-native platform architecture. It sounds technical, but the idea is to make verification part of the system from the start. The setup brings together Aadhaar-enabled identity checks, DigiLocker document workflows, behavioural analytics, and a hybrid uncertainty-aware trust scoring method. That trust part is built using Bayesian updating, Subjective Logic, and Dempster-Shafer Theory, plus PCR6 for Proportional Conflict Redistribution. The whole point is to use India’s Digital Public Infrastructure, and not just as a “nice-to-have”. Instead, the framework tries to line up incentives across landlords, tenants, brokers, and platforms by steering attention toward transaction utility rather than advertising revenue. A few testable hypotheses are proposed, especially ones about reduced search friction and better market efficiency overall. Finally, there are broader implications discussed for PropTech in emerging economies, where trust and coordination tend to be the real bottlenecks.

title: Does a Stricter Significance Threshold Improve Replication?

detail.title: Does a Stricter Significance Threshold Improve Replication?
detail.abstract: Motivated by the replication crisis, some disciplines have adopted higher thresholds for statistical significance. Financial economics may follow. We ask whether a universally higher threshold improves replication. Defining the replication rate RR(c) = P(T 2 > c | T 1 > c), we show it strictly decreases under a unimodal effect distribution whenever the replication study is no larger than the original. Under a bimodal one, with true nulls as the second mode, RR(c) rises only above a critical null fraction we derive. The rise holds only up to a threshold, beyond which it falls again. Raising the threshold is thus unlikely to improve replication except in narrow cases.

title: When Timing Matters: Compounding Floods and Supply-chain Losses in Cambodia
affiliations: International Institute of Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA) and

detail.title: When Timing Matters: Compounding Floods and Supply-chain Losses in Cambodia
detail.abstract: Floods are among the most destructive hazards in Southeast Asia, and Cambodia is particularly exposed. While their direct damages to households and infrastructure are regularly reported, their broader economic consequences remain poorly quantified. Two gaps stand out: direct damage assessments are rarely integrated with indirect impact modeling, and there is little evidence on how compound events amplify economic disruption. We address both by coupling the open-source risk platform CLIMADA with DisruptSC, a spatially explicit agent-based model of supply chains. Using input-output tables and data on firms and households, we map economic flows onto Cambodia's transport network and quantify how flood-induced road disruptions propagate through supply chains. Building on the 2023 wet season, we simulate what-if scenarios for single-basin and multi-basin floods that occur simultaneously or in succession. Isolated disruptions generate moderate household losses, mainly through price increases from longer routing, but losses grow nonlinearly as inventories deplete and shortages spread. Summing single-basin impacts markedly misestimates the losses of simultaneous multi-basin flooding: the interaction of shocks matters as much as their magnitude. In cascading scenarios, losses rise sharply once successive events occur faster than inventories can be restored, revealing a tipping point in the timing between events. Compound flooding can thus trigger systemic supply-chain impacts even when physical damage is limited. Risk assessments and resilience planning should therefore consider not only infrastructure exposure but also the economic interdependencies that can turn localized floods into national disruptions.

title: Damming Trade Volatility

detail.title: Damming Trade Volatility
detail.abstract: and Law Abstract：This paper studies the causal impact of shipping stability on firm-level export volatility. We exploit the impoundment and navigation of the Three Gorges Dam (TGD) as an exogenous shock that reduced inland shipping costs and improved transport reliability. Using matched Chinese Industrial Enterprise and Customs data from 2001 to 2011, we implement a difference-indifferences design. We find that improved shipping conditions reduce export volatility by about 9.7% (equally 0.21 standard deviations). Heterogeneity analyses show that the stabilizing effects are concentrated among non-state-owned firms, general trade exporters, and firms serving geographically proximate markets. The effect is stronger for firms with greater reliance on waterway transport, supporting the interpretation that the decline in export volatility operates through improved inland shipping conditions. Mechanism analyses show that shipping stability promotes export diversification across destinations, mitigates rainfall-induced disruptions to inland waterway transport, and that improved transport conditions reduce firms' inventories and accelerate inventory turnover. Our findings underscore the critical role of transport infrastructure in enhancing trade stability and economic resilience in developing countries.

title: From Investors' Voice to Firm Value: Evidence on Complaint Resolution and Firm Risk in India
affiliations: and Indian Institute of Management (IIM), Indore

detail.title: From Investors' Voice to Firm Value: Evidence on Complaint Resolution and Firm Risk in India
detail.abstract:
We investigate whether resolving investor complaints is an external corporate governance mechanism that improves firm value. Using a hand-collected panel of 7,245 firm-year observations of 779 firms listed on the National Stock Exchange (NSE) of India during 2011-2021, we investigate the relationship between investor complaint resolution and firm value measured by Tobin's Q. We find that a successful resolution of investor grievances demonstrates managerial accountability and responsiveness, increases investor confidence, reduces information asymmetry and mitigates agency conflicts, thereby increasing firm value drawing on agency, stakeholder, signalling and information asymmetry theories. The empirical results show that firms with higher investor complaint resolution rates (ICRR) are associated with significantly higher market valuation. Additional analyses show that resolving investor complaints substitutes for weak internal governance, indicating that external investor monitoring is more valuable when internal governance mechanisms are relatively weak. In contrast, the positive valuation effects of complaint resolution are attenuated among highly leveraged firms. We further examine the underlying mechanism and find that effective complaint resolution significantly reduces firm risk, thereby increasing firm value. These findings suggest that lower firm risk constitutes an important channel through which investor complaint resolution creates shareholder value. The results remain robust when using the logarithm of investor complaints received as an alternative proxy for investor voice and after addressing observable and unobservable selection bias and endogeneity using kernel propensity score matching, the Heckman two-stage selection model, and dynamic system
GMM estimation. Overall, this study extends the corporate governance literature by
demonstrating that investor complaint resolution is not merely a regulatory compliance activity
but an effective external governance mechanism that substitutes for weak internal governance
and enhances firm value by reducing risk.

title: The Right to be Wrong  - Infrastructure and Complexity
affiliations: University of Birmingham

detail.title: The Right to be Wrong  - Infrastructure and Complexity
detail.abstract: Human progress exists between two conditions: the limits of knowing and the necessity of acting. Mathematics reveals this tension most clearly. The search for foundations eventually reaches rules that cannot themselves be justified through an infinite search for deeper rules. ZFC captures this disciplined humility. Humanity has the right to be wrong, but only after fulfilling the obligation to ask. Infrastructure gives this obligation practical urgency. Roads, energy systems, cities, and digital networks are decisions made on behalf of others and across generations. The question is therefore not whether uncertainty exists. The question is whether society has searched deeply enough before accepting uncertainty. This paper traces that search through the structure of knowing itself. The Poisson bracket sits at the centre of humanity's most successful architecture for understanding change: locating a system, understanding its motion, and studying its evolution. Yet human systems create a deeper challenge. They observe, interpret, and adapt. The system changes through the knowledge produced about it. Cost-benefit analysis is examined within this context. It represented a powerful layer of inquiry, bringing discipline and comparison into public decisions. However, when infrastructure transforms systems rather than simply producing impacts, CBA reaches its boundary. The challenge is not calculation, but the assumption that transformation can be reduced to measurement within a stable world. Drawing on Layered Operator Appraisal (LOA), this paper argues that infrastructure appraisal must itself become layered. Infrastructure should be understood as an operator transforming the State-Market-Society field, while preserving conventional appraisal where its assumptions hold. The future of appraisal is therefore not the search for perfect prediction, but a deeper organisation of understanding.

title: Who "We" are Matters: The Influence of Organizational Identity Orientation on Public Participation in Government
affiliations: Northern Illinois University and

detail.title: Who "We" are Matters: The Influence of Organizational Identity Orientation on Public Participation in Government
detail.abstract: Public participation in government remains far from ubiquitous despite calls for a modern administrative state defined by co-production. This research offers a new perspective on public participation by considering the relationship between organizational identity orientation (OIO) managerial views of the process and the frequency of engagement between local governments, citizens, and nonprofits. Results show that in collectivistic public organizations, managers view participation as an important responsibility, even when it creates organizational inefficiencies. No direct link between OIO and frequency of participation is found. These findings point to a nuanced relationship between OIO, managerial beliefs, and organizational action.

detail.abstract: The relationship between the quality and durability of political regimes and human damage due to interpersonal violence is evaluated econometrically. Some economic theories of violence propose that the quality of government allows for the solution of problems without the powerful resorting to violence. Hence, the hypotheses investigated are whether longerlasting regimes with better quality of governance are associated with less human harm from interpersonal violence. Fixed-effect and instrumental variable models are used. A consistent relationship is found between the durability of the political regime and lower damages due to interpersonal violence, but there is no relationship between higher quality of the regime and violence. Among the problems of internal validity, the possible endogeneity of the variable that measures the quality of government stands out.

title: The Deposit Franchise and the Risk-taking Channel of Monetary Policy
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Imperial College Business School and

detail.title: The Deposit Franchise and the Risk-taking Channel of Monetary Policy
detail.abstract: Why does the same monetary tightening lead some banks to write safer loans than others? We develop a model and identify a novel deposit-franchise mechanism within the risk-taking channel of monetary policy. Sticky deposits generate rents that vanish if the bank fails, giving low-deposit-beta banks more skin in the game. The model predicts that tightening lowers the payoff to risk-taking, so banks with a stronger deposit franchise cut risk more because failure destroys larger rents. We test this prediction using the Federal Reserve's confidential loan-level data, interacting high-frequency monetary policy surprises with predetermined deposit betas in specifications with bank and borrower-time fixed effects. Our findings show that monetary tightening reduces risk-taking, especially at low-beta banks, and the result survives a horse race with bank capital. New-loan originations reveal how banks de-risk: for the same borrower-quarter, low-beta banks originate loans that are more likely to be collateralised and senior.

title: Alcohol Use Among Women and Its Association with Caesarean Section Delivery Outcomes in India
affiliations: Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Roorkee and Imperial College London

detail.title: Alcohol Use Among Women and Its Association with Caesarean Section Delivery Outcomes in India

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: No financial or funding grants received in order to carry out this study.

detail.abstract: Background: Rising caesarean section (CS) rates in India have increased the need to distinguish between elective and emergency procedures. Although alcohol use among women has been linked to adverse perinatal outcomes, its association with CS delivery type remains underexplored. This study examines the relationship between women's alcohol use and elective and emergency CS deliveries in India. Methods: We used data from the fifth round of the National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5, 2019-21), which covered 232,657 women who had an institutional delivery in the preceding five years. Delivery outcomes were classified as normal delivery, elective CS, and emergency CS. Women's alcohol use was the key explanatory variable. Sociodemographic, economic, and geographic covariates were included as controls. Prevalence patterns were examined using GIS maps, and multinomial logistic regression was used to estimate associations. Results: Alcohol use among women was associated with a higher relative likelihood of both elective CS (RRR 1.49, 95% CI 1.30-1.70) and emergency CS (RRR 1.57, 95% CI 1.36-1.81). The association was stronger for emergency CS, while wealth and education were more strongly associated with elective CS. Conclusion: Women's alcohol use is associated with CS delivery type, particularly emergency CS, highlighting the need for alcohol screening during antenatal care.

title: AI Procurement and AI in Procurement
affiliations: Bristol University Law School

detail.title: AI Procurement and AI in Procurement
detail.abstract: Procurement is the gateway for public sector AI adoption, as well as an area of active experimentation with AI. Both 'AI procurement' and 'AI in procurement' are giving rise to emerging regulatory and governance strategies and practices that shed light on the challenges and constraints of current approaches to 'digital transformation'. This contribution explores emerging trends and identifies areas for future research, with a specific focus on the promotion of responsible and trustworthy AI adoption. In relation to AI procurement, it discusses 'contractbased' and 'standard-based' approaches to its governance, as well as the emerging pivot towards prescriptive AI procurement legislation. In relation to AI in procurement, it explores the emergence of safe harbours and persistent challenges for AI use by public buyers, and maps some of the challenges arising from bidders' (improper) AI use. It concludes by bringing together themes from the two related issues of procuring AI and using AI in procurement.

title: Discounted Deterrence: How a Cut in the Price of a Violation Reshaped Workplace-safety Enforcement

detail.title: Discounted Deterrence: How a Cut in the Price of a Violation Reshaped Workplace-safety Enforcement
detail.abstract: In July 2025 the U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration raised the penalty discount for establishments with 11 to 25 employees from 60 to 70 percent, a roughly 25 percent cut in the expected penalty, and left every other size band unchanged. Using the full federal enforcement record, this paper estimates the effect on the violations the agency cited. Cited violations per programmed inspection at the treated band fell by about a fifth to a third, with precise zeros at every unmoved band, and the decline survived placebo policy dates, a nevertreated state-plan comparison, a targeting check, and a citation-timing battery. Worker injury data reject a safety improvement as large as the citation decline would imply and show no improvement even at a small fraction of that size. Because a price cut moves both a firm's compliance incentive and the enforcer's own citing behavior in the same direction, the enforcement record decouples from compliance, and independent harm data are required to adjudicate. The evidence is consistent with enforcement forbearance rather than improved compliance, though the decisive injury year is not yet available. The findings caution against reading enforcement counts as compliance when a sanction price has moved.

title: The Gendered Roles in Society and Women's Leadership in Higher Educational Institutions: The Graham Gender Equality Theory and Scale

detail.title: The Gendered Roles in Society and Women's Leadership in Higher Educational Institutions: The Graham Gender Equality Theory and Scale
detail.abstract: Gender equality is a fundamental human right and a prerequisite for achieving equality of outcomes for both men and women in terms of education, labor markets, etc., At the same time, gender roles are barriers to women's career advancements and attainment of leadership positions. Gender disparity is a typical problem in higher education institutions. Women are still underrepresented in leadership in higher education institutions. This study employed an inductive approach in collecting data. This study followed the systematic literature review and the integrative literature review methods in developing knowledge about the sources of gender disparities in leadership in higher education institutions and the measures that are relevant in creating gender equality in leadership in higher education institutions. The findings from this study indicate that women face three main challenges in attaining leadership in higher education institutions. These are sociocultural elements, organizational and institutional elements, and individual elements. The findings also indicate that eradicating gender disparities in leadership can be achieved when organizational leaders have an accurate understanding of the root causes of gender disparities in leadership and implement measures to reduce or eliminate the problems. The measures include formulating and implementing policies, strategies, and interventions. This article presents new ideas about the paths to achieving gender equality in leadership; the Graham Gender Equality Theory, Model, and Scale. The gendered systems in society and in many organizations can be analyzed by using the Graham Gender Equality Scale. The level of gender disparities in the workplace and the key elements that lead to gender disparities can be evaluated using the scale. This study presents some practical implications for human resources managers and organizational leaders and some research focus, propositions, theories, and model to guide researchers in extending knowledge about gender disparities and gender equality in leadership.

title: The Green Revolving Door: Talent Flows Under Environmental Regulation
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen - School of Management and Economics,  and Macquarie University

detail.title: The Green Revolving Door: Talent Flows Under Environmental Regulation
detail.abstract: We examine how firms reorganize regulator-specific human capital in response to measurement-intensive environmental disclosure requirements. Exploiting the implementation of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program (GHGRP), we document a sharp increase in EPA-experienced hiring among treated firms, incremental to firms' general green labor demand. This effect is stronger among firms with weaker internal environmental capabilities and sufficient financial resources. In terms of hiring composition, firms primarily hire junior technical and legal-compliance personnel rather than senior government-relations staff, consistent with firms seeking operational and regulatory expertise rather than political capital. In addition, we document reductions in Scope 1 carbon emissions among high emitters, alongside improvements in carbon accounting quality. EPA hiring is also associated with fewer environmental violations among high-risk firms; however, we find no evidence of lower penalties conditional on violations. Overall, the evidence is more consistent with knowledge transfer than with regulatory capture.

title: Acceptance Drives Growth
affiliations: IIM SAMBALPUR

detail.title: Acceptance Drives Growth
detail.abstract:
An organisation's acceptance gives people a sense of belonging and purpose. When an organisation values people for who they are, respects their ideas, and gives them equal opportunities to grow, they feel confident and motivated. Employees do their best work when they know they are trusted, supported, and appreciated. A workplace built on acceptance creates teamwork, innovation, and lasting success. When people feel accepted, they don't just work for an organisation, they grow with it.

Just like a mother gives unconditional love, a father provides strength and support, a teacher guides us towards growth, and a friend stands with us through every situation, an organisation should create a sense of acceptance and belonging. When an organisation respects people, trusts their abilities, and provides opportunities to grow, employees feel valued and motivated. This acceptance may not be unconditional like family, but it is built on mutual respect, contribution, and shared goals. A truly great organisation becomes a place where people feel they belong and can achieve their full potential.

 

In today’s rapidly evolving professional environment, organisations must prioritise integrity, innovation, accountability, and teamwork. These values are essential for achieving sustainable growth and long-term success. A strong organisational culture enhances employee performance, drives operational excellence, and strengthens competitiveness in a dynamic business landscape. Modern businesses increasingly recognise the importance of ethical leadership, strategic management, and continuous improvement in building resilient and future-ready organisations. This article highlights the significance of professional values, collaboration, and strategic management in building a productive and future-ready organisation. It further discusses how collective responsibility and visionary leadership contribute to organisational development and societal progress.

Acceptance is one of the most important yet least discussed factors influencing professional growth. In professional life, acceptance means understanding responsibilities, adapting to change, learning from failures, and aligning individual goals with organisational objectives. Growth in an workplace is closely connected to acceptance at every level. A new company starts with uncertainty, limited resources, and a strong vision, where acceptance is about risk-taking, trust-building, and patience. An existing company entering the next stage of growth faces different challenges such as scaling operations, culture transformation, leadership shifts, and managing complexity.

title: A Case Study Framework for 5S Implementation in Material Management at a Construction Warehouse
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: A Case Study Framework for 5S Implementation in Material Management at a Construction Warehouse

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This is my first case study author by me only
declarations.ethicsApproval: case study for warehouse management
declarations.funderStatement: My self funded for this

detail.abstract: Construction warehouses are frequently affected by poor material organization, inventory inaccuracies, excessive material search time, avoidable material damage, and safety hazards, all of which contribute to project delays and cost overruns. This paper presents a structured case study framework for applying the 5S methodology (Sort, Set in Order, Shine, Standardize, Sustain) to improve material management in a construction warehouse. The study outlines a phased implementation approach and evaluates performance using five key performance indicators (KPIs): material search time, inventory accuracy, warehouse space utilization, material damage rate, and 5S audit score. Using illustrative before-and-after data consistent with outcomes reported in comparable lean-warehouse studies, the paper demonstrates the anticipated magnitude of improvement achievable through disciplined 5S implementation. The case organization is anonymized as "Company X," a mid-sized residential and commercial real estate developer based in Bengaluru, India. Findings suggest that sustained 5S practice, supported by management commitment and workforce training, can materially reduce search time and material loss while improving inventory reliability and site safety. The paper concludes with practical recommendations for scaling 5S across multi-site warehouse operations and identifies directions for future empirical research.

title: Interaction Dynamics in Professional Teams: A Physics-Based Analysis of 35 Corporate Project Teams

detail.title: Interaction Dynamics in Professional Teams: A Physics-Based Analysis of 35 Corporate Project Teams

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses only publicly available, fully anonymised data from the QMSum dataset (Zhong et al., NAACL 2021). No human participants were recruited or interacted with. All speaker identities in the dataset are replaced with role labels (Project Manager, Marketing, Industrial Designer, User Interface) by the original dataset creators. No ethics approval is required.

detail.abstract: We applied Hermion's proprietary physics-based interaction intelligence engine to 35 real corporate product teams drawn from the QMSum meeting corpus-a publicly available dataset of annotated multi-actor professional conversations. Each team was tracked longitudinally across a full project lifecycle (kick-off through conclusion), producing a single continuous interaction arc per team. Across 385 intelligence runs and three studies, we find that: (1) professional team dynamics are measurable at the structural level without reading message content; (2) the Project Manager amplifies peak interaction dynamics by +10.5 percentage points over equivalent Marketing pairings-a gap invisible at aggregate level; (3) the direct PM/UI designer dyad produces the highest average peak of any pairing (25.5%), above the executive pair and above PM versus the full team; (4) peak dynamics cluster in the development phase of the project lifecycle, producing a 4.2x gap between peak and current progression at project conclusion; (5) structural friction is the universal primary resistance type across all 35 teams; and (6) 48% of teams show detectable cross-actor mismatch before decline events. All analysis was conducted without transmitting or storing message content.

title: Partner Alcohol Use and Women's Access to Healthcare Services in India
affiliations: Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Roorkee and Imperial College London

detail.title: Partner Alcohol Use and Women's Access to Healthcare Services in India

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: No financial or funding grants received in order to carry out this study.

detail.abstract: Background: Despite policy efforts to improve maternal health in India, many women continue to face barriers in accessing healthcare. While structural and socio-cultural determinants have been widely studied, behavioural factors, particularly those related to male partner characteristics, remain largely underexplored. This study examines whether partnerrelated alcohol characteristics are associated with women's healthcare access barriers and whether this relationship is influenced by state-level alcohol control policies. Methods: We analysed data from the fifth round of India's National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5), including 46,154 currently married women. The outcome was a binary indicator capturing whether women reported any barriers in accessing healthcare services. We used logistic model to assess the association between partner alcohol consumption and healthcare access barriers, adjusting for individual, partner, and household characteristics. Results: Around 42% of women reported at least one barrier to care, and 27% had partners who consumed alcohol. Partner alcohol use was significantly associated with greater odds of reporting barriers (OR = 1.53; 95% CI: 1.19-1.97). Additionally, women in states with alcohol prohibition policies had lower odds of reporting barriers (OR = 0.94; 95% CI: 0.88-0.99), suggesting some policy effect. Conclusion: Male partner alcohol consumption is a significant behavioural determinant of women's access to healthcare in India. The findings highlight that interventions targeting both partner behaviour and policy environments may be critical in reducing barriers to health care access in India.

title: Human Dignity and the Innocent Agent
affiliations: Ono Academic College Faculty of Law

detail.title: Human Dignity and the Innocent Agent
detail.abstract: Courts and commentators do not differentiate between defendants who perpetrate crimes by means of inanimate weapons or trained animals and those who perpetrate crimes by means of other human beings used as innocent agents. I argue that this widely accepted comparability is grossly insensitive to the violation of the human dignity of the person whom the perpetrator has turned into an instrument to an offence. Identifying the innocent agent as a possible second victim of the offence alongside the intended victim raises several issues of both morality and law. First, the question of moral pertinence: do the scenarios that the law recognises as cases of innocent agency involve a violation of the dignity of the innocent agent? Second, the question of criminalisation: is it appropriate to invoke criminal law to protect the dignity of the innocent agent? Third, the question of the protected interest: assuming that both the dignity of the innocent agent and their autonomy are compromised, which of these violations is graver? I argue that there is a strong connection between the doctrine of innocent agency and the violation of the dignity of the innocent agent; that the violation of the innocent agent's dignity is severe enough to warrant criminalisation and that this is simple enough to enforce; and that the injury to the innocent agent's dignity is more significant than the injury to their autonomy. The operative proposal of this article is that the law should recognise perpetration by means of innocent agents as an aggravated mode of commission or an aggravating factor in punishment.

title: Policy Implementation and Congressional Rhetoric: Evidence from the Affordable Care Act
affiliations: Bocconi University and Bocconi University

detail.title: Policy Implementation and Congressional Rhetoric: Evidence from the Affordable Care Act
detail.abstract: How does policy implementation change the rhetoric elected officials use to connect policy to economic outcomes? We study Medicaid expansion under the Affordable Care Act, whose staggered state rollout changed the local policy environment facing members of the U.S. House. Linking implementation timing to 1.6 million tweets from 2012 to 2019, we measure insurance premium mentions and cross-party semantic similarity in ACA rhetoric within states. Before implementation, both parties linked the ACA to premiums, but with opposite valence. During implementation, however, supporters moved away from that link: Democrats reduced ACA-premium co-mentions by about 3.5 percentage points over two years, while Republicans did not; moreover, cross-party semantic similarity rose by about one-half of a standard deviation. These shifts occur even though the ACA is associated with lower premium growth in expansion states. The evidence suggests that implementation can narrow supporters' rhetorical possibilities even when a policy is associated with its intended outcomes.

title: All-Digital Phase-Locked Loop Design for Phase Noise Improvement Using Model Predictive Controller and TDC-DTC at S-Band
affiliations: Shahed University and Shahed University

detail.title: All-Digital Phase-Locked Loop Design for Phase Noise Improvement Using Model Predictive Controller and TDC-DTC at S-Band
detail.abstract: This paper presents the design of a fully digital phase-locked loop (ADPLL) aimed at improving phase noise performance in frequency synthesizers. The proposed system integrates a digital frequency-phase detector using a Time-to-Digital Converter (TDC) and a Digital-to-Time Converter (DTC), alongside a digital loop filter employing a Model Predictive Controller (MPC). The design achieves a phase noise of -118.54 dBc/Hz at a 1 kHz offset and -152.93 dBc/Hz at a 1 MHz offset with a center frequency of 3 GHz. The system demonstrates a lock time of 500 ns and spur levels reaching -92 dBc. The entire architecture was simulated using MATLAB Simulink and is suitable for FPGA implementation in future work.

title: Right To Information Act:  A Critical and Empirical Study of the Right to Information Act, 2005, its 2019 and 2023 Amendments, and its Institutional Performance in India
affiliations: Independent Legal Researcher

detail.title: Right To Information Act:  A Critical and Empirical Study of the Right to Information Act, 2005, its 2019 and 2023 Amendments, and its Institutional Performance in India

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract:
Citizens in a democracy can only hold their government accountable if they know what it is doing. The Right to Information Act, 2005 gives Indian citizens a legal route to information held by public authorities, and this paper examines how that right took shape, how it has been used, and where it now stands after two significant legislative amendments. 
The paper traces the RTI movement's history in India, the court decisions that built its constitutional foundation, the Act's key provisions, and the practical process for filing a request. It critically examines the Right to Information (Amendment) Act, 2019 and the 2023 amendment to Section 8(1)(j) introduced through the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, and asks whether these changes have weakened the institutional independence and disclosure mandate the original Act was built on. Drawing on recent Central Information Commission and Satark Nagrik Sangathan data (2019–2025), it also assesses the Act's practical performance — application volumes, pendency, and enforcement — against its statutory design. 
The RTI Act has undeniably opened up Indian governance in ways that were not possible before 2005. But its record is uneven, and the paper argues that recent amendments have compounded, rather than resolved, the implementation problems that already existed. Closing that gap will require both administrative reform and a legislative course correction, not further dilution of the disclosure mandate.

title: Social Choice and Market Choice: On the Normative Value of Private Contracts in Antitrust Analysis
affiliations: University of Tübingen - Faculty of Law

detail.title: Social Choice and Market Choice: On the Normative Value of Private Contracts in Antitrust Analysis
detail.abstract: This article argues that private law contracts have a normative value which warrants stronger recognition in antitrust law. It investigates the function of contracts on markets as a choice mechanism. The analysis, then, traces the legal history of private law contracts, starting in ancient Roman law, over canon law and natural law theory, heeding their influence on continental European law as well as on common law doctrine. This historical viewpoint, in conjunction with an account of the systemic role of contracts in markets, demonstrates how freedom of contract has a normative value which warrants stronger recognition in modern counterfactual antitrust analysis. The normative value lies in the fact that contractual autonomy empowers individuals, including those who constitute numerical minorities, to pursue personal rather than collective ends. From there, the article adopts a critical stance towards modern approaches that seek to expand antitrust doctrine by incorporating societal goals and values outside consumer welfare.

title: In Search of Balance: Climate Policy and Energy Security in the Brics Countries

detail.title: In Search of Balance: Climate Policy and Energy Security in the Brics Countries
detail.abstract: Nowadays BRICS is playing more and more significant role in the world economy, strengthening its economic and energy potential. A vital direction of both the forum's agenda as a whole and the policy of each country in particular is the implementation of climate commitments. However, sometimes proactive modernization of energy systems can cause serious risks for state energy security. Therefore, this study delves into the search for the solution of this dilemma both at the country and forum levels. Keywords.

title: The Hidden Cost of Food-Drug Interactions in Medicare Advantage Populations: A Case for Pharmacist-Led Culturally Adapted Intervention

detail.abstract: Medicare Advantage plans bear substantial and largely unquantified financial risk from food-drug interactions (FDIs ) among their enrolled populations. Older adults managing multiple chronic conditions — particularly those from West African, Caribbean, South Asian, East Asian, Middle Eastern, and Latin American communities — face disproportionate FDI risk due to the absence of culturally adapted guidance tools. This white paper presents a pharmacoeconomic framework quantifying the cost burden of FDI-related hospitalizations, emergency department visits, and medication non-adherence within Medicare Advantage populations. The author introduces MediMeal Safe as a pharmacist-led, culturally adapted digital intervention and proposes a value-based contracting model for Medicare Advantage plan adoption. A NIH SBIR Phase I feasibility study (PAR-24-138, NIA, $299,998) is under submission for September 2026.

title: Institutional Decoupling in Emerging Markets: The Audit Paradox and Digitalisation Gap in Turkish Cooperatives
affiliations: Ordu University

detail.title: Institutional Decoupling in Emerging Markets: The Audit Paradox and Digitalisation Gap in Turkish Cooperatives
detail.abstract: This study examines institutional decoupling in Turkish cooperative governance by focusing on the gap between the formal alignment of cooperative legislation with global governance principles and functional shortcomings in practice. Using qualitative document analysis, it compares national legislation and recent policy documents (including the Türkiye Cooperativism Strategy and Action Plan (2025-2029) and the Specialised Commission Report) with international standards (ICA principles and ILO Recommendation No. 193). Findings indicate substantial de jure convergence consistent with isomorphic pressures in New Institutional Theory, yet persistent de facto deviation in auditing and digitalisation mechanisms. This macro-micro paradox is also visible in international benchmarks. Although Türkiye ranks 17th globally by nominal GDP, no cooperative appears in the WCM Top 300 by absolute turnover, and only one (Trakya Birlik, rank 272) is listed in the turnover/GDP per capita ranking. From an Agency Theory perspective, member-elected internal audit bodies often lack professional competence, weakening oversight and accountability-an "audit paradox"-while slow digitalisation (e.g., KOOPBİS) and bureaucratic fragmentation reinforce a "digitalisation gap." The article argues that Türkiye's cooperative potential requires governance reform that professionalises auditing while preserving democratic participation and consolidates the fragmented framework into a coherent, digitally supported oversight regime.

title: Post -Crisis Financial Security Architecture in the Face of the 2023 Crisis Episode

detail.title: Post -Crisis Financial Security Architecture in the Face of the 2023 Crisis Episode

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific funding.

detail.abstract: The aim of this article is to analyse the 2023 crisis episode-the failures of regional US banks-from the perspective of the effectiveness of the post-crisis financial safety architecture developed in the aftermath of the 2008 global financial crisis. Drawing on a review of the literature and regulatory documents, the article reconstructs the sequence of events, identifies their causes, and confronts them with the paradigms underlying modern banking supervision. The analysis shows that the banks involved in the crisis episode met their capital requirements and, in many cases, their liquidity requiremen ts as well. The source of the problems lay in qualitative factors: poor risk management, unsustainable business models, and inadequate supervision. The episode also revealed a new mechanics of banking crises-social media and digital banking compressed the timeline of deposit runs from days to hours, fundamentally altering the dynamics of tail risk events. The article's main conclusion is that the existing regulatory framework, built on the paradigm of normally distributed phenomena and quantitative risk measures, is ill-suited to this new reality. Distribution tails are fatter, and future crises may be more violent and harder to contain than previously assumed. The 2023 episode, though limited in scale, should be treated as a warning signal for the financial safety system as a whole.

title: The Central Bank Theater: Measuring the Narrative Dependency of the Federal Reserve, 1996-2026
affiliations: Comillas Pontifical University

detail.title: The Central Bank Theater: Measuring the Narrative Dependency of the Federal Reserve, 1996-2026
detail.abstract: Central bank communication has shifted from describing the economy to managing expectations about it. We introduce the Narrative Dependency Index (NDI), defined as the ratio of forward-guidance sentences to economic-data sentences in Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) minutes, and compute it over 70,848 sentences drawn from all 242 FOMC meetings between January 1996 and April 2026. Sentences are classified with a zeroshot large language model pipeline whose reliability is established by a dual validation protocol: inter-model agreement (Cohen's = 0.90) and human-model agreement (= κ κ 0.99). Formal multiple-breakpoint tests identify four structural breaks-May 2005, December 2012, January 2016, and June 2020-that partition three decades of Fed communication into five regimes whose boundaries coincide with documented institutional turning points, including the adoption of quantitative thresholds and the postliftoff normalization. Narrative dependency peaks in the 2013-2016 regime (mean NDI = 0.74) and collapses during crises: the index reaches its historical minimum in August 2010 and falls to its lowest level in fifteen years in April 2026, amid the oil-supply shock. Eventstudy regressions show that narrative surprises move long-term Treasury yields but not the short end, while unconditional effects on equity volatility are indistinguishable from zero. Performative communication, we conclude, is a fair-weather instrument: it flourishes when promises are cheap and retreats precisely when markets would need it most.

title: From Solvency Selection to Too-Big-to-Break: Architecture, Events and Reversibility in Capital Centralisation

detail.title: From Solvency Selection to Too-Big-to-Break: Architecture, Events and Reversibility in Capital Centralisation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that he has no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study did not involve human participants, personal data, animals, or clinical interventions; therefore, ethics approval and informed consent were not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Research on capital centralisation has converted a classical proposition of political economy into an empirical programme: monetary and financial conditions select capitals asymmetrically, shape acquisition capacity and target vulnerability, and thereby reorganise ownership and control. This working paper synthesises three recent developments. The first retains the scalar concentration statistic but treats the control operator as the primary measurement object, making the statistic one projection of the structure of command. The second classifies the primitive events that transform that structure-strong merger, accretive acquisition, transfer of an existing stake, pure divestiture and legal split-and derives testable signatures for four frontiers. The third studies the formation, persistence and reversibility of control blocks through a coagulation-fragmentation process. The synthesis separates concentration from centralisation, formation from persistence, and legal break-up from restored autonomy. It yields an integrated empirical programme: replicate the established measure; reconstruct the control operator; classify events; estimate acquisition intensity and size selectivity together with fragmentation intensity and scalability; and follow entities after break-up. Monetary policy, competition policy, resolution and corporate law then jointly shape the extent, form and reversibility of capital centralisation.

title: MuniVIX: Implied Volatility and Stress Regimes in the Municipal Bond Market
affiliations: University of Chicago, Harris School of Public Policy, Center for Municipal Finance

detail.title: MuniVIX: Implied Volatility and Stress Regimes in the Municipal Bond Market
detail.abstract: We construct a daily municipal bond implied volatility index ("MuniVIX") built from puts and calls on municipal bond exchange-traded funds (ETFs). We then decompose MuniVIX into a Treasury rate volatility component and an orthogonal residual, and show that residual ("Municipal-Specific Volatility Index" or MSVI) is a statistically and economically significant regime classifier for municipal market stress. In market stress episodes that originate in the municipal market, the MSVI leads Treasury volatility by one to six weeks. The MSVI also predicts municipal ETF outflows even after controlling for lagged flows and rate changes. The municipal-specific volatility channel carries incremental information about stress origins beyond what MOVE alone provides. For practitioners and policymakers monitoring municipal market access, MuniVIX and the MSVI offer a daily, forward-looking complement to the yield-spread and transaction-cost measures that currently dominate the toolkit.

title: Transfer Entropy for Cross-Asset Order Flow Contagion: A KSG Analysis and the Limits of Small-Sample Predictive Validation

detail.title: Transfer Entropy for Cross-Asset Order Flow Contagion: A KSG Analysis and the Limits of Small-Sample Predictive Validation
detail.abstract: Cross-asset contagion analysis has traditionally relied on tools that are either symmetric by construction (Pearson correlation) or bound to a fixed-order linear functional form (Granger causality). This paper develops, from first principles, a Kraskov-Stögbauer-Grassberger (KSG) estimator of Transfer Entropy to measure directional, nonlinear information flow between SPY and QQQ order flow, proxied by a tick-rule-based Directional Volume Imbalance (DVI). We document five iterations of increasing methodological rigor: (1) naive linear baselines, which carry almost no directional information under lagged cross-correlation, though a Granger F-test does detect a significant asymmetry; (2) a histogram-binned Transfer Entropy estimator, implemented specifically to test its stability, whose sign and magnitude we show empirically to be unstable across arbitrary bin-count choices; (3) the KSG estimator itself, validated against synthetic ground truth using an independent-noise case and a known coupled autoregressive process; (4) application to real 1-minute SPY/QQQ order flow, with an empirically window-tuned rolling Net Contagion Signal; and (5) a downstream LSTM ablation study testing whether this signal improves 5-minute-ahead return forecasts. A single training run appears favourable to the Transfer Entropy feature; repeating the experiment across fifteen random seeds shows this result does not survive: neither the RMSE nor directional-F1 differences are statistically distinguishable from zero under a paired t-test, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, or bootstrap confidence interval. We conclude that KSG Transfer Entropy is a methodologically sound, bin-free tool for detecting genuine structural lead-lag relationships, and that it converges with Granger causality on the qualitative direction of SPY-to-QQQ order-flow leadership in our sample, but that translating this structural signal into a statistically defensible predictive edge requires substantially more data than an eight-trading-day pilot sample can support. We frame this as a cautionary methodological finding on the risk of single-run ablation studies in small financial datasets, of direct relevance to practitioners evaluating novel signals before capital deployment.

title: Beyond CAGR: A Risk-Adjusted Information Ratio for SIP Investors in Indian Equity Mutual Funds
affiliations: and

detail.title: Beyond CAGR: A Risk-Adjusted Information Ratio for SIP Investors in Indian Equity Mutual Funds
detail.abstract: India's mutual fund industry services ten crore (100 million) systematic investment plan (SIP) investors. Yet, fund performance across the industry continues to be evaluated through time-weighted, lump-sum measures. Money-weighted returns are well understood in principle, but they are rarely quoted in practice and are absent from risk-adjusted evaluations. This paper brings them into the information ratio framework. We scale the excess return (XIRR) of a monthly SIP over its benchmark by the fund's tracking error and compute the SIP information ratio (SIPIR). We then compare it with its conventional lump-sum counterpart (CAGRIR) computed on identical windows with an identical denominator and study their difference, a risk-adjusted sequence effect. Across 6,497 rolling five-year windows of 98 Indian equity funds (2015-2026), with Driscoll-Kraay inference addressing the design dependence, we observe that the aggregate sequence effect is zero, but category-level differences are reliably positive for large-cap funds (+0.060) and reliably negative for small-cap funds (-0.121). The two measures return opposite verdicts on whether a fund added value in 15.1 percent of windows, with the direction of disagreement predictable from the category. CAGR-based ratings systematically understate large-cap and overstate small-cap performance for the dominant Indian retail investment mode.

title: Digital Distance in the Data Gravity Model -Measure and Evidence
affiliations: Kyungpook National University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Digital Distance in the Data Gravity Model -Measure and Evidence
