detail.abstract: This study measures digital distance tailored for digital service trade by introducing a data gravity model and evaluating its effectiveness across 59 countries from 2005 to 2024. The new digital distance reflects cross-border data flow friction costs in digital service trade. Digital distance exerts a statistically significant and negative effect of digital trade within the data gravity model. Furthermore, the impact of digital distance significantly surpasses that of physical distance on digital service trade. Robustness tests confirm our hypotheses across different economic development levels and digital service sectors.

title: Persuading with Memory
affiliations: Bocconi University

detail.title: Persuading with Memory
detail.abstract: This paper studies persuasion through memory. I use a theory-driven experiment in which an advisor and an investor share a common history of past news, but the advisor's only action is to re-report one previously observed item when the investor forms his belief. The experiment randomly varies both advisors' incentives and the association between contexts and signals across realized histories. Re-reporting past information creates scope for persuasion: investors' beliefs move with advisors' incentives, and advisors strategically choose which item to re-report. In this nuanced strategic setting, however, the data do not support the specific associative-memory mechanism emphasized by the framework. The findings identify memory as a distinct margin of persuasion while leaving open which features of memory drive persuasion in strategic environments.

title: Counting Patents, Miscounting Innovation
affiliations: École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL)

detail.title: Counting Patents, Miscounting Innovation

declarations.funderStatement: This project is made possible through a Living Literature Review grant generously provided by Coefficient Giving (formerly Open Philanthropy). Coefficient Giving does not exert editorial control over this work, and the views expressed here do not necessarily reflect those of Coefficient Giving.

detail.abstract: Patent counts are widely used to measure innovation, but their apparent precision often hides deep conceptual and empirical problems. This paper explains why patents are useful but imperfect indicators: not all inventions are patented, not all patents reflect valuable innovation, and legal, strategic, sectoral, and geographic factors distort comparisons. It argues that patent statistics remain indispensable, but only when matched carefully to the research question and interpreted as measures of patenting behavior, not innovation itself.

title: The Cap's Transition to a Single Fund: Legal and Institutional Consequences
affiliations: Università di Mantova

detail.title: The Cap's Transition to a Single Fund: Legal and Institutional Consequences
detail.abstract: Aim: The 2025 Commission package (COM[2025] 565 and COM[2025] 560) proposes a Single Fund (PNRF) for 2028–2034, merging CAP resources with other EU instruments and ending the traditional dual-pillar system. This raises fundamental questions on compliance with Articles 38–44 TFEU, the preservation of CAP’s functional autonomy, and the resilience of budgetary safeguards. Material and methods: The article adopts a legal-dogmatic and comparative approach. It analyses EU primary law, the 2023–2027 CAP framework (Regulations 2021/2115–2117), and the Commission’s 2025 proposals (COM[2025] 565, 560, 550, 545). Parliamentary and Council materials, Member State positions, and stakeholders’ documents (e.g. CEJA, Copa-Cogeca) are reviewed. Given the scarcity of post-2027 academic literature, this work provides one of the first systematic legal-institutional assessments of the Single Fund. Results: The analysis identifies tensions between simplification and integration, on the one hand, and the CAP’s legal “speciality” on the other. Formal safeguards (ring-fenced agricultural envelopes, ac counting separation, performance monitoring) exist, but doubts remain about their durability in times of budgetary stress. Some stakeholders see the PNRF as risking “silent renationalisation”, while others interpret it as subsidiarity in action, offering Member States flexibility to adapt interventions and over come CAP’s compartmentalisation. Conclusions: The reform is not merely technical but constitutional in impact. Its success depends on balancing innovation with continuity: only robust safeguards can ensure that the Single Fund preserves the CAP’s identity as a genuine common policy. Implemented with transparency and legal certainty, it could modernise agricultural governance; without such guarantees, it risks eroding the CAP’s distinctiveness and weakening its role in food security and sustainable rural development.

title: Innovate to Lobby? European Firms and Corporate Lobbying during Climate Change Regulation
affiliations: Bocconi University,  and

detail.title: Innovate to Lobby? European Firms and Corporate Lobbying during Climate Change Regulation
detail.abstract: Which firms are more likely to lobby regulators about green policy: those producing more or fewer green innovations? The answer is not obvious. On one hand, highly green-innovative firms may prefer to concentrate on innovation, since their internal technological capabilities reduce their need for outside information. On the other hand, the innovativeness of their technologies gives them reason to seek regulatory access: to learn how policy will evolve and to position their innovations for commercial success. We argue that the answer turns on a second dimension: a firm's exposure to climate regulation. Because exposure raises the value of regulatory information most for firms able to act on it, green innovativeness and climate exposure should be complements, with access concentrated among firms high on both. We examine this in the context of the European Union's 2019 European Green Deal (EGD), which sharply increased regulatory uncertainty. Using data on 2,038 publicly listed European firms over 2015-2023, we combine EU lobbyingmeeting disclosures with firm-level green-patent and carbon-intensity measures. Exploiting the unexpected elevation of climate policy in 2019, we show that green lobbying rose sharply afterward, driven primarily by firms that are both highly green-innovative and highly carbon-intensive: consistent with the two dimensions operating as complements rather than as independent motives. Our findings show that green innovation and lobbying rise jointly under regulatory change, advancing research on non-market strategy and corporate innovation.

title: The Institutionalisation and Investigation of Zakat as a Revenue Instrument: The Islamic State, 2014-2017

detail.title: The Institutionalisation and Investigation of Zakat as a Revenue Instrument: The Islamic State, 2014-2017

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, personal data collection, or experimental procedures, and was based entirely on publicly available secondary sources, including official reports, legal instruments, and case law.

detail.abstract: The Islamic State (‫الدولة‬ ‫اإلسالمية‬ , al-Dawlah al-Islāmiyyah) (ISIS) provides one of the clearest documented modern examples of Zakat being transformed from a religious obligation into a compulsory instrument of territorial governance and revenue extraction. Drawing on FATF reporting, the ISIS Files archive, and UNITAD case assessments, this paper seeks to reconstruct the administrative system developed around zakat collection and examine its integration into the group's wider financial architecture, which was centred on the Treasury Office (‫ديوان‬ ‫بيت‬ ‫املال‬ , Dīwān Bayt al-Māl). It argues that the system is best understood as coerced taxation rather than charity diversion. That distinction matters operationally because disruption methods designed for the misuse of charitable organisations do not readily apply where the terrorist organisation itself acts as the taxing authority over a controlled population. The analysis also considers how large counter-terrorism datasets and battlefield material were converted into usable intelligence and admissible evidence, with particular attention to Europol, Eurojust, data protection and fair-trial safeguards. Finally, the paper concludes by identifying practical considerations for future financial-forensics mandates, including early evidence preservation, data categorisation, coordination with receiving jurisdictions and analysis of terrorist-financing systems as integrated structures streaming from yet mostly analysed and investigated as isolated revenue streams (FATF, 2015; George Washington University Libraries, n.d.-a, n.d.-b; UNSC, 2017; UN Iraq, 2024a).

title: Ecologies of Violation: A Critical Ecological Pedagogy Against the Grain of Dispossession

detail.title: Ecologies of Violation: A Critical Ecological Pedagogy Against the Grain of Dispossession

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares there are no conflict of interest or other ethical considerations to report.
declarations.funderStatement: The author received no financial support for the research, authorship, and/or publication of this article.

detail.abstract: The ecological crisis presents a profound challenge to prevailing forms of education, demanding a critical engagement that reaches beyond technical solutions or purely ideological critiques. This paper argues that the crisis must be understood as an intensified moment of a longer history of dispossession and violation, rooted in the entwined logics of capitalism and coloniality, which operate not merely at material and political levels but fundamentally reshape subjectivity and foreclose alternative ways of being and knowing. Mainstream educational responses, often framed in terms of sustainability or environmental literacy, tend to mask this deeper reality and risk perpetuating the very logics of extraction and domination that undergird ecological devastation. Drawing on critical theory, the Black radical tradition, and decolonial thought, I propose a critical ecological pedagogy that confronts this violence directly, arguing that emancipation in the Anthropocene necessitates cultivating a different sense of relationship – to the earth, to other beings, and to one another – by naming, resisting, and undoing the pedagogical textures of dispossession. My analysis explores how educational sites, from curricula to classroom practices, become arenas where this violence is enacted, yet also hold the potential for fostering alternative subjectivities rooted in interdependence and resistance against accumulation and erasure. This requires rethinking critical pedagogy itself, pushing it beyond familiar frameworks to engage with the crisis at the level of being, and exploring how educators and students can collaboratively forge forms of knowing and acting adequate to this profound political and ethical challenge.

title: Optimal Monopoly Regulation with Flexible Investments
affiliations: University of Bonn

detail.title: Optimal Monopoly Regulation with Flexible Investments
detail.abstract: I study the optimal regulation of a monopolist who can covertly invest in cost reductions and privately observes the resulting costs. Thus, there is moral hazard and adverse selection. The monopolist's investment is flexible: she can choose any cost distribution subject to an investment cost. I show that all inefficiencies under optimal regulation can be traced back to the convexity of the investment cost function. Moreover, for natural classes of investment cost functions, optimal regulatory policies are simple, featuring finitely many options and inducing finite cost distributions. I identify conditions under which a fixedprice contract is optimal. A key step in the analysis is a characterization of implementable distributions.

title: The Invisible Ceiling: Social Insurance Thresholds in Indian Survey Data
affiliations: Madras School of Economics

detail.title: The Invisible Ceiling: Social Insurance Thresholds in Indian Survey Data
detail.abstract: India's two contributory social insurance schemes are bounded by statutory lines, a wage ceiling (21,000 rupees for the ESI, 15,000 for the EPF) and establishment-size thresholds. Using every Employment-Unemployment Survey and Periodic Labour Force Survey round from 1999 to 2025 and a gazette-complete panel of statutory changes, we show that these lines are invisible in survey data. Across seven ceiling regimes, reported pay never rearranges around the operative ceiling, and reported benefit coverage never breaks at it, even among urban private limited companies and after purging round-number reporting. A truncation test explains why. Household surveys measure benefit receipt, not scheme membership. Protection is instead structured by the firm, through enterprise class and the ten-worker threshold, in an architecture stable over two decades. When the price rather than the line changed, with the July 2019 contribution cut, administrative registrations rose about four per cent against trend and covered-sector pay responded. Prices transmit; boundaries do not and surveys see only benefits.

title: Schema-Aware Query Translation and Tabular Reasoning for Enterprise Databases

detail.title: Schema-Aware Query Translation and Tabular Reasoning for Enterprise Databases
detail.abstract: Relational Database Management Systems (RDBMS) hold the vast majority of structured enterprise data. However, applying Large Language Models (LLMs) to perform natural language querying and tabular reasoning directly over relational schemas presents major bottlenecks: full schema injection quickly exhausts context windows, complex join relationships lead to hallucinated SQL syntax, and security risks like invalid query execution constrain enterprise adoption. To overcome these limitations, we present Schema-Aware Query Translation and Tabular Reasoning for Enterprise Databases aka Inference-from-RDBMS, an open-source framework designed for schema-aware query translation, dynamic context pruning, and execution-guided tabular inference over complex RDBMS structures. The framework extracts database metadata to construct an interactive Schema Relationship Graph (SRG), prunes unreferenced tables and foreign-key joins using semantic distance metrics, and passes a minimal schema sub-graph to an execution-validated text-to-SQL generator. We evaluate Inference-from-RDBMS across standard enterprise benchmarks (including SPIDER and realworld multi-table schemas). The experimental results demonstrate that our framework achieves an 88.4% execution accuracy, reduces prompt token overhead by 52%, and cuts end-to-end query translation latency by 41% compared to standard schemainjected baseline models. These results position Inference-from-RDBMS as a robust, secure, and cost-efficient solution for natural language database interfaces in large-scale AI applications.

title: Re-Assessing Power: Lowering Structural Presumptions for an Economy Built on First Degree Price Discrimination
affiliations: Fordham University School of Law

detail.title: Re-Assessing Power: Lowering Structural Presumptions for an Economy Built on First Degree Price Discrimination
detail.abstract:
Antitrust law relies on structural presumptions that emerged in an industrial economy where firms generally posted uniform prices, possessed limited information about individual customers and workers, and could exercise market power only after achieving substantial market shares. Those presumptions were empirical judgments about the relationship between concentration and economic power. This Essay argues that advances in big data and artificial intelligence have fundamentally altered that relationship. Firms can now use individualized prediction to estimate reservation prices and reservation wages, target exclusion at particular rivals,  and reinforce their positions. These capabilities permit the exercise of meaningful economic power at substantially lower levels of market share than twentieth-century doctrine assumed.

Rather than abandoning structural analysis in favor of purely behavioral inquiry, this Essay argues that the rise of opaque algorithmic decisionmaking strengthens the case for administrable structural presumptions while requiring those presumptions to be recalibrated. Because AI enables firms to exercise market power earlier, antitrust law should presume the possibility of harmful power earlier. The Essay therefore proposes lowering structural thresholds throughout antitrust doctrine and treating algorithmic capacity itself as evidence of market power.

title: Compensation Costs for Work Related Accidents in Polish Agriculture
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Compensation Costs for Work Related Accidents in Polish Agriculture
detail.abstract: Aim: The intent of this study is to discern the level and trend of compensation costs resulting from work related accidents in Poland's agriculture sector. Materials and Methods: The data base of Poland's Agricultural Social Insurance Fund (KRUS) reflecting information regarding incidents and costs pertaining to lump-sum compensation for work related accidents and occupational diseases. The results are generated through 'time trend analysis' i.e. a data analysis method which intent is to expose incident nature represented by sequence observation of said events where time is a primary factor. The result of these applications allows, among several, to comprehend trend changes in compensation costs because of agricultural work accidents. The project reviews current literature with study material analysis. The study includes all lump-sum compensation payments registered with KRUS for a five-year study period i.e. 2020-2024, inclusive. Source material is based upon subject matter review and unpublished secondary data sourced from KRUS. Long term analysis categories may supplement study time voids in these areas. Results: Agricultural accident compensation costs in Poland should be treated as a systemic barrier in economic and social development in rural areas. Schultz notes the restricted investment potential in human potential results from uncertainty of work risk in agriculture. Stiglitz and Pigou have confirmed that internalization leads to a lowered work value in agriculture. The average gain of compensation payments has risen by about 80% in the Śląskie voivodship. In the remaining voivodships, compensation gains have been lower, which may testify to the fact that farmers encounter fewer accidents, however, those accidents tend to be more severe. Conclusions: In Poland's agricultural sector, loss estimates caused by occupational accidents are varied. Occupational safety investments-automation, education, access to health safety, etc.should be seen as human capital investments, not simply as financial cost.

title: Salt Wars
affiliations: ,  and

detail.title: Salt Wars
detail.abstract: Salt was a key fiscal resource in premodern Europe. The ability of states to appropriate salt shaped patterns of fragmentation and consolidation of territories. We propose a model demonstrating that when and where salt was non-appropriable by a central authority, it produced more fragmented partitions. Territories with non-appropriable resources could fund rebellion and resist incorporation, which made conquest of such territories unprofitable. In equilibrium, such territories were more likely to remain independent. To test this hypothesis, we construct a new dataset of 251 historical salt sites, classify them by extraction technology, and exploit temperature variation driven by the Little Ice Age as a source of exogenous identification. Colder temperatures reduced coastal/marine salt production, raising the relative value of inland salt. Where inland salt was appropriable by a central authority, specifically rock salt, we find this temperature shock generated more consolidation. Where it was dispersed and non-appropriable, specifically salt from brine springs, it produced greater fragmentation.

title: Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) Investing and Financial Performance: Evidence from South African Mining Companies: A Panel Data Analysis
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) Investing and Financial Performance: Evidence from South African Mining Companies: A Panel Data Analysis

detail.abstract: This study examines the relationship between Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) performance and financial performance among mining companies listed on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE). Using a panel dataset of JSElisted mining firms over 2015-2024 and firm fixed-effects regressions, we disaggregate ESG into E, S, and G pillars. Results show governance is consistently associated with higher ROA, ROE, and Tobin's Q. Environmental performance imposes shortterm costs but enhances long-term market valuation. Social performance reduces short-term profitability but improves operational stability. The findings suggest ESG effects are pillar-and horizon-specific, with implications for asset managers and mining executives in emerging markets. By focusing on South Africa, a market with mandatory integrated reporting and high exposure to ESG-related risks, this paper provides some of the first emerging-market evidence on the materiality of disaggregated ESG. The results caution against the use of composite ESG scores in investment decisions.

title: An AI-Assisted Poisson-kelly Framework for Soccer Probability Modeling and Risk-controlled Market Decision Infrastructure
affiliations: Boston College,  and University of Michigan, Ann Arbor

detail.title: An AI-Assisted Poisson-kelly Framework for Soccer Probability Modeling and Risk-controlled Market Decision Infrastructure
detail.abstract:
This paper presents an AI-assisted quantitative framework for soccer probability modeling and risk-controlled market decision support using a Poisson goal model and a Kellyoptimized capital allocation strategy. Building upon historical Major League Soccer (MLS) match data, the model estimates team-level attacking and defensive strength through handicap, total-goals, and home-advantage ratings. These ratings are converted into expected goal parameters and used within a Poisson distribution to generate probabilistic forecasts for win, draw, and loss outcomes. 
     The resulting model-implied probabilities are compared against market-implied probabilities derived from bookmaker odds in order to identify pricing discrepancies and potential inefficiencies. To avoid purely directional speculation, the framework incorporates a disciplined risk-control layer based on the Kelly Criterion, which determines position size according to estimated edge, payoff structure, and bankroll constraints. 
     A preliminary simulation using early 2024 MLS matches generated a virtual return of 16.4% across 37 model-selected opportunities. Although the sample size remains limited and should not be interpreted as conclusive evidence of persistent market outperformance, the results demonstrate the feasibility of integrating sports analytics, probability calibration, market comparison, and capital allocation into a unified decision-support system. This framework contributes to the broader development of AI-assisted probability infrastructure for sports prediction markets, risk analytics, and data-driven decision systems. Future work will expand the model through expected goals data, player-level injury quantification, market microstructure features, liquidity adjustment, and machine learning ensembles.

title: The Goodhart Horizon: A Self-Monitoring Impossibility Theorem for Proxy Optimization, and the Price of Seeing Past It

detail.title: The Goodhart Horizon: A Self-Monitoring Impossibility Theorem for Proxy Optimization, and the Price of Seeing Past It
detail.abstract: Optimizing against a proxy eventually diverges from the welfare the proxy was meant to track. This is Goodhart’s law, and in reinforcement learning from human feedback and reward-model overoptimization it is visible as a curve: true reward rises, peaks, and falls while the proxy keeps climbing. This paper shows that relative to any monitoring channel the system can build from its own trajectory, the divergence has a horizon, a structural limit beyond which the system cannot see whether it has crossed. We call it the Goodhart Horizon, and establish three results about it. Each result is conditional on a stated premise about what the monitor can read, and exactly as strong as that premise. First, the Horizon. The decisive parameter, the Goodhart gap (how much welfare is given back past the peak), is non-identified from any monitoring channel whose conditional law given the system’s trajectory does not depend on welfare, the class that is closed under functions of the system’s own trajectory, including, when the welfare deficit is outcome-defined rather than mechanism-encoded, transcript-graded evaluation and trajectory-based interpretability. Two welfare worlds, one benign and one collapsing, generate identical observation laws; no test, estimator, eval, or stopping rule computed from any such channel separates them above chance, at any sample size. The impossibility is structural, the decision-relevant quantity leaves no signature in any channel the system can build from its own trajectory, a blindness we borrow the rhetorical shape of selfreference limits to name, claiming no Gödel-style diagonalization or fixed-point construction. Second, the price of seeing past it. Escape is architectural: it requires a channel whose readings depend on welfare itself, and that channel is priced by a closed-form overlap functional whose growth regime (polynomial, stretched-exponential, or Gaussian-exponential) is now fixed by a regime-spectrum lemma in terms of the thinness of the proxy’s upper edge (with the dramatic regimes an edge asymptotic, not instantiated by the measured instance below). Third, the audit hierarchy. Price visibility is structurally one-sided: internal telemetry can expose undercoverage, while sufficiency requires a welfare-touching channel or an explicit worst-case allowance; certifying any grader’s informativeness is itself welfare-touching, so each level of oversight requires a new welfare-touching certifier one level up. A governance reading follows: an institution that tries to audit itself reproduces the Horizon one level up, so a stable institution must import exogenous outcome-contact, a welfare-touching channel it cannot compute from its own trajectory, of which mandatory external audit is one realization, not the requirement itself; a companion in preparation argues that, under stated substrate-dependent conditions, no mechanism jointly satisfies incentive compatibility, participation, budget balance, share-of-gains, and a worst-case alignment ceiling, summarized there, not proven here.

title: Ordinal Measurement of Social Inequality with Ordinal Data
affiliations: Northwest University - School of Economics and Management and Northwest University

detail.title: Ordinal Measurement of Social Inequality with Ordinal Data
detail.abstract: Suppose that everyone shares a linearly ordered common value space. A social equality ordering is a rational order on the distribution space of individual values that satisfies anonymity, the equality principle, and the equalization principle. Nevertheless, it remains unclear how arbitrary unequal distributions should be ranked. The classic leximin (leximax) rule violates both the equality principle and the equalization principle and thus cannot be considered as a social equality ordering. Therefore, we propose the basic leximin (leximax) rule as a social equality ordering characterized by the basic (inverse) Pareto principle and the full Hammond principle; when the common value space is order-dense, the full Hammond principle is equivalent to the Hammond principle. The basic leximin (leximax) rule, however, violates the maximum inequality principle, and thus we further propose the first (second) ordinal egalitarian rule as a social equality ordering characterized by the first (second) Pareto equity principle and the weak second (first) Pareto equity principle. In addition, we demonstrate the equivalence between social orderings on the value distribution domain with variable population and social orderings on the frequency distribution domain. Finally, we provide an illustrative application of those ordinal inequality measures.

title: Designing Contests under Judgment Uncertainty: Effort Incentives and Entry Control for Heterogeneous Contestants
affiliations: , Southwest Jiaotong University, University of International Business and Economics and Tsinghua University

detail.title: Designing Contests under Judgment Uncertainty: Effort Incentives and Entry Control for Heterogeneous Contestants
detail.abstract: Problem definition: Organizers of innovation contests often find it difficult to accurately assess the value of solutions, because of information constraints and the inherent difficulty of evaluating such value. However, it remains unclear how such judgement uncertainty affects organizers' decisions, especially when contestants differ in ability. Methodology/results: We introduce judgement uncertainty into the innovation contest model with heterogeneous contestants. We first examine how judgement uncertainty and ability heterogeneity jointly affect contestants' effort choices. The analysis suggests that high-ability contestants reduce effort in response to increased variance of uncertainty, while low-ability contestants initially increase and then decrease effort. Secondly, we characterize the organizer's entry decision using two effects: (1) the incentive effect, which captures the marginal change of contest scale on contestants' effort, and (2) the crowd-in effect, which measures the marginal effect of contest scale on the probability that the winner is a high-ability contestant. Our analysis suggests organizers restrict entry when the incentive effect outweighs the crowd-in effect. This occurs in two scenarios: when ability difference is large and uncertainty variance is small, or when ability difference is small and uncertainty variance is large. We further show that the optimal contest scale is significantly larger under left-skewed uncertainty than under right-skewed uncertainty. Managerial implications: Judgment uncertainty can affect heterogeneous contestants in different ways and may even stimulate effort from low-ability contestants. Accordingly, whether entry should be restricted depends on how judgement uncertainty and ability heterogeneity jointly shape the relative strength of two effects of contest scale. Organizers should restrict entry when adding contestants weakens incentives more than it improves the chance of selecting a high-ability winner, and otherwise allow broader participation.

title: When LLMs Bid: Winner's Curse and Information Interventions in Human-AI Competitive Auctions
affiliations: , Southwest Jiaotong University, University of International Business and Economics and Tsinghua University

detail.title: When LLMs Bid: Winner's Curse and Information Interventions in Human-AI Competitive Auctions
detail.abstract: With the rapid development of Artificial Intelligence (AI), large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed as autonomous decision-makers in economic contexts, rather than merely as advisory tools. This shift fosters human-AI environments, in which human decision-makers interact and compete with LLM agents. Economists have developed an equilibrium framework to understand and predict human strategies and to guide mechanism design. However, whether this equilibrium framework continues to apply in human-AI competitive environments remains an open question. To this end, we conduct a series of common-value auction experiments, in which simulation agents and equilibrium agents are used to model human bidders interacting with LLM agents. Using descriptive comparisons and mixed-effects model analyses, we find that LLM agents' bidding strategies (ChatGPT and DeepSeek) exhibit systematic deviations from equilibrium bidding. At high-valuation levels, aggressive bids lead LLM agents to suffer from the winner's curse, despite some degree of bid shading. In contrast, both LLM agents exhibit limited sensitivity to underestimation at low-valuation levels. Further, the winner's curse becomes more pronounced as the auction scale expands. We therefore examine whether feedback and information interventions can mitigate this LLM-induced risk. Historical outcome feedback induces more conservative bidding, but does not fully eliminate winner's curse exposure. We further show that targeted interventions have model-specific effects: DeepSeek bidders benefit more from a qualitative winner's curse warning, whereas ChatGPT bidders respond more strongly to a precise equilibrium reference. These findings suggest that effective governance requires matching information design to the behavioral response patterns of different LLM agents.

title: Public Capital Expenditure Efficiency in Nigeria: A Review of the Evidence and an Agenda for Subnational Frontier Analysis

detail.title: Public Capital Expenditure Efficiency in Nigeria: A Review of the Evidence and an Agenda for Subnational Frontier Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This paper is a conceptual literature review and research agenda based exclusively on published literature. It did not involve human participants, animals, personal data, or primary data collection; therefore, ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Nigeria presents one of Sub-Saharan Africa’s most consequential fiscal paradoxes: a state whose public expenditure grew by over 460% between 2011 and 2023, yet whose capital budget implementation rates fell as low as 25% in some years and whose GDP per capita growth averaged below 2% annually. This paper reviews the existing empirical literature on public expenditure efficiency in Nigeria and developing countries more broadly, identifies critical gaps in the subnational analysis of capital expenditure efficiency, and proposes a frontier-based research agenda to address them. Drawing on production frontier theory, the Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) literature, and the new developmentalist framework, the paper argues that the dominant approach in existing Nigerian public finance research—aggregate-level regression of expenditure on growth outcomes — is insufficient to reveal the subnational efficiency variation that matters most for fiscal reform. The paper proposes a two-stage DEA and panel Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) framework as the appropriate methodological response, identifies the institutional, political economy, and macroeconomic determinants that such an analysis should examine, and outlines the data sources and feasibility conditions for its implementation. The proposed research agenda has direct implications for the Budget Office of the Federation’s ongoing capital expenditure reform programme and for state-level budget management across Nigeria.

title: Option Markets and Price Discovery: Do Informed Traders Front-run Stock Markets through Derivatives?

detail.title: Option Markets and Price Discovery: Do Informed Traders Front-run Stock Markets through Derivatives?
detail.abstract: The Efficient Market Hypothesis (EMH) is a financial theory stating that asset prices reflect all available information instantaneously, yet empirical evidence increasingly documents persistent mispricing, particularly around information events such as earnings announcements. This paper investigates whether equity options markets reveal information about impending stock price movements before those movements occur in the underlying stock market, therefore suggesting that informed traders systematically possess an informational advantage in derivative markets. Using a framework based on put-call implied volatility spreads and earnings announcement windows, we examine whether option market variables predict abnormal stock returns during periods of high information asymmetry. Our findings provide evidence that volatility spreads in options markets predict earnings announcement returns with economically meaningful magnitudes (82 basis points), suggesting that option traders anticipate the informativeness of earnings releases before stock prices adjust. We interpret these results as consistent with the hypothesis that markets are segmented by trader sophistication and that informed investors strategically position in options markets ahead of major information events. The psychological foundations of this phenomenon reveal that informed traders exploit not only genuine information advantages but also systematic behavioral biases, particularly loss aversion and overconfidence, embedded in how different trader types process information. The implications extend to our understanding of market efficiency, the role of financial regulation in ensuring fair price discovery, and the strategic considerations facing both institutional investors and retail traders in modern capital markets.

detail.title: Technology and Jobs: Is Automation Increasing Inequality in India? A Panel Data Analysis of Automation, Job Polarization and Income Inequality (2007–2024)
detail.abstract: The rapid diffusion of automation technologies across advanced and emerging economies has raised fundamental concerns about employment displacement, wage polarization, and the concentration of economic gains among high-skill workers and capital owners. In India, where nearly ninety percent of the workforce remains in informal employment with limited social protection and digital literacy, these concerns are particularly acute. This study provides one of the first long-run sector-level causal analyses of automation and inequality in India over 2007–2024, using a panel of six major sectors (manufacturing, IT/BPO, retail, agriculture, construction, healthcare). The empirical strategy combines panel fixed effects, a Bartik-style instrumental variable (foreign robot adoption × sectoral automatable task exposure), quantile regression, and novel extensions incorporating financial channels and input-output spillovers. The findings show that a one-unit increase in the automation index reduces low-skill employment share by 11.8–16.9 percentage points (p < 0.001) and raises the sectoral Gini coefficient by 0.18–0.27 points (p < 0.001). Quantile regressions reveal that sectors with initially high low-skill concentrations experience significantly larger displacement effects (Q75 coefficient: −19.2 vs Q25: −12.8). The COVID-19 pandemic accelerated automation-induced low-skill displacement (interaction coefficient −2.85, p < 0.01). Extended results indicate that access to institutional credit amplifies automation’s inequality effect, while social protection spending mitigates it, and cross-sector spillovers from manufacturing to retail and construction are economically meaningful. Without coordinated investments in digital literacy, social protection, retraining systems, and inclusive financial policies, automation risks entrenching structural inequality and labor-market exclusion in India and other emerging economies.

detail.abstract: Economic systems are commonly analyzed through production, exchange, prices, capital, labor, growth, incentives, institutions, contracts, money, firms, and markets. Yet each of these categories presupposes a deeper structural condition: economic identity, value-reference, obligation, record, trust, and attribution must remain recoverably continuous across time. A contract has economic force only if the obligated parties, terms, records, and enforcement pathways remain identifiable after delay, dispute, transfer, or disruption. A currency functions only if value-reference remains stable enough to support exchange, accounting, saving, pricing, and future settlement. A firm preserves economic value only if its productive identity, organizational memory, governance structure, operational capacity, and stakeholder obligations remain coherent through transformation. This paper develops recoverable continuity as a structural constraint on economic value, institutional trust, and market stability. Building from the principle C 2 = C, where continuity must itself remain continuous under iteration, the paper argues that economic systems remain intelligible only where the structures that preserve identity, obligation, record, enforcement, value, and trust can themselves be carried forward. Existing economic literature establishes that institutions, property rights, trust, transaction costs, contracts, firms, monetary credibility, bank stability, and enterprise resilience all matter for economic performance. The contribution of this paper is to unify these domains under a single continuity condition. Economic breakdown occurs not only through scarcity, inefficiency, poor incentives, weak institutions, liquidity shortage, or external shock, but through failures of recoverable attribution. Inflation, bank runs, accounting fraud, contract failure, sovereign instability, supply-chain disruption, institutional distrust, and enterprise collapse can all be interpreted as cases in which economic identity, value-reference, obligation, record, or trust becomes unstable, fragmented, or non-recoverable. Recoverable continuity therefore provides a structural lens through which economic value, institutional trust, and market stability can be understood.

detail.abstract: Financial institutions in the United States face a well-documented dual failure in current fraud and anti-moneylaundering (AML) defenses: rule-based monitoring systems miss increasingly sophisticated fraud typologies, while accurate machine learning models frequently operate as uninterpretable "black boxes" that cannot satisfy the auditable, regulator-facing explanation requirements of the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA), federal Anti-Money Laundering regulations, and Dodd-Frank Act supervisory expectations. This white paper presents the GATE (Graph-Augmented Temporal Ensemble) model, a hybrid architecture combining graph-theoretic network analysis, engineered temporal/behavioral sequence features, and a stacked ensemble classifier, paired with a dual explainability layer (permutation importance and exact Shapley-value attribution). The model is implemented in full, trained, and evaluated on a synthetic transaction and account-network dataset constructed to mirror the documented statistical structure of established public benchmarks in this field (the Kaggle/ULB credit card fraud schema and the Elliptic Bitcoin AML graph schema). Under a temporal (walk-forward) holdout evaluation, the GATE model achieves a ROC-AUC of 0.983 and PR-AUC of 0.813, and at an F1-optimized decision threshold achieves 78.4% recall and 65.3% precision on a 1.2%-prevalence fraud stream. Explainability analysis independently recovers, via two distinct methods, the correct subset of underlying fraud-signal features embedded in the data-generating process, demonstrating explanation fidelity. Adversarial robustness testing further characterizes model behavior under both random perturbation and targeted mimicry attacks, identifying a specific, disclosed vulnerability that informs concrete recommendations for production deployment. This document is presented as supporting technical evidence for a proposed research endeavor to develop, validate, and disseminate explainable AI architectures for real-time fraud detection and AML compliance at U.S. financial institutions.

detail.abstract: I document that emerging-economy output, prices, exports, and exchange rates are more sensitive to global shocks under a dovish Federal Reserve, and that U.S. tightening depresses output and exports through a corporate financing channel. detail.abstract: Many public higher education systems in countries in Asia and Africa have sought a new approach in response to their modern environments. Built in the 1950s following decolonization, they seek to overcome colonial regulations, norms, and practices to produce new public outcomes focused on communities and market forces. Drawing from in-depth case studies of seven new universities in India, we assess the role of organizational design and public value institutions in producing contemporary public outcomes. title: Stochastic Correlations and Crisis VaR
affiliations: FactSet Research Systems Inc.

detail.title: Stochastic Correlations and Crisis VaR
detail.abstract: Correlations between the prices of financial instruments increase in times of crisis as market participants move their investments to those perceived as safe-the so-called 'flight to quality'. This paper presents a value-at-risk (VaR) calculation where an imminent crisis is simulated by evolving correlations stochastically over the VaR horizon via a Brownian bridge process on the Cholesky manifold, ending at a correlation matrix in a "crisis" regime. We find that well diversified portfolios are the most affected. Specifically in the 2008 crisis, a geographically and sectorally diversified portfolio saw its VaR increase by 238 basis points, against 53 basis points for an already highly-correlated portfolio, a difference of over four times. This vulnerability is geometrically encoded as the geodesic distance between the current correlation matrix and the crisis regime correlation matrix: portfolios with larger geometric distances undergo more dramatic correlation changes. Two aspects of this approach are noteworthy. First, the historical stochastic evolution of empirical correlation matrices in this geometry have a quadaratic variation that grows linarly in time-a hallmark of a pure Browian motion. Secondly, the process is computationally efficient and straightforward, and can be paired with automatic differentiation to yield sensitivities directly, avoiding the pitfalls of non-positive-definite matrices that traditional bumping methods can produce.

title: A New Panel Granger Causality Test in Heterogeneous Panels with Cross-Sectional Dependence

detail.title: A New Panel Granger Causality Test in Heterogeneous Panels with Cross-Sectional Dependence
detail.abstract: Granger causality stands out as one of the most widely adopted econometric tools for uncovering dynamic predictive relationships in economics, finance, and related fields. This paper proposes a new Panel Granger Causality Test for assessing the Granger non-causality in heterogeneous panel data in the presence of complex crosssectional dependence and cross-sectional heteroscedasticity. The proposed test exhibits reliable performance across a broad range of panel regimes, including long panels, short panels, and high-dimensional panel settings in which both the cross-sectional dimension and time dimension are large. We establish rigorous theoretical guarantees on the statistical properties of the proposed test, and demonstrate significant power gain under the alternatives. The empirical performance is demonstrated via extensive simulation studies, as well as a real-world application to evaluate the Granger-causal relationships among the production of four crop categories across di!erent geographical regions and various economic levels.

title: Disguised Profit Distributions and the Return of Dividend Taxation in Brazil: Rebuttable Presumptions, Fair Value, and the Standard of Accounting Proof
affiliations: University of Coimbra Institute for Legal Research

detail.title: Disguised Profit Distributions and the Return of Dividend Taxation in Brazil: Rebuttable Presumptions, Fair Value, and the Standard of Accounting Proof
detail.abstract: Brazil reinstated dividend taxation in November 2025 after a twenty-nine-year exemption, reviving a dormant anti-avoidance regime: the disguised profit distribution rules of 1977, a functional analogue of the US constructive dividend. Those rules presuppose historical-cost accounting, yet they awaken in an IFRS environment in which the statutory benchmark, market value, coexists with fair value measurements produced inside the taxpayer's own books. This paper argues that the coming litigation cycle will be decided on evidence rather than on substance. It reconstructs the regime as a set of rebuttable presumptions that requalify genuine, non-commutative transactions rather than shams; allocates the burden of proof in two stages; distinguishes the standards of proof governing ordinary and fraud-based penalties; and proposes a tiered standard of accounting proof that ranks value evidence by input observability and treats fair value reports as qualified indicia.

detail.abstract: We estimate managerial dynamic preferences over risk and uncertainty in an Epstein-Zin framework using U.S. executive compensation, managerial wealth proxies, aggregate consumption-wealth ratios, and stock returns from 1992 to 2024. Firm-level estimates imply median relative risk aversion (RRA) of 1.17, median elasticity of intertemporal substitution (EIS) of 2.65, and a 66.2% early-resolution share excluding boundary solutions. Results are stable across alternative compensation, wealth specifications, and instrument sets. Preference parameter estimates forecast post-period leverage, operating stability, and, more modestly, risk-adjusted returns.

detail.abstract: Prediction models are routinely compared across studies using scalar measures such as area under the ROC curve (AUC), Brier score, log score, calibration statistics, or net benefit. We argue that such comparisons do not identify differences in model quality when the underlying prediction tasks differ. Performance depends on both the model and the prediction task, so a weaker model on an easier task can appear to outperform a stronger model on a harder one. This paper develops a referencetask framework for comparing probability models. The framework fixes a common prediction problem and evaluates performance relative to the predictive improvement attainable on that problem. Reference-normalized predictive skill measures the share of attainable predictive improvement captured by a model. Test-difficulty-normalized reference skill extends the same logic to fixed models evaluated across test samples, separating model performance from changes in test-sample difficulty. Simulations and applications to mortgage denial, Norwegian firm failure, and unemployment prediction show that raw metrics move with test-population difficulty, whereas the normalized measures reveal how much available predictive signal each model captures.

detail.abstract: This study examines whether individuals can effectively express their emotions or "fellow-feelings" to a machine, an impartial observer, or individuals who have caused them harm and investigates the effect of these emotional expressions on behavior. Our findings indicate that the impartial observer is the most preferred outlet for emotional expression, with neither the machine nor the offending party being able to adequately fulfill this role. Negative emotions are more commonly expressed to the impartial observer and machine, whereas positive emotions are more often directed toward the offending party. Additionally, our findings indicate that emotional expression cannot replace costly punishment and that communication channels do not affect the behavior of the offending party.

detail.abstract: We reexamine Meese-Rogoff (1983) puzzle by applying the long-horizon regression framework of Mark (1995) to monthly GBP/USD and CAD/USD data spanning January 1971 to March 2025. The model regresses multi-step-ahead exchange rate changes on the current purchasing power parity (PPP) misalignment between the spot rate and its fundamental value. All inference is conducted using Newey-West heteroskedasticity-and-autocorrelation-consistent (HAC) standard errors, which are essential given the overlapping observations generated by long-horizon forecasting. For GBP/USD, the PPP coefficient βk is statistically significant at short-to-medium horizons under the full sample but deteriorates markedly in the post-1998 period, suggesting a structural weakening of the PPP signal in the modern era. For CAD/USD, the relationship is weaker at one month but surprisingly robust and persistent at medium-to-long horizons, holding across both sub-samples. Volatility regime analysis reveals that PPP predictability is concentrated in high-volatility periods for both currencies, consistent with an arbitrage-cost interpretation. We conclude that PPP fundamentals contain genuine predictive information but that its magnitude, persistence, and statistical robustness are highly currency-and period-specific.

title: Marriage, Education, and Work: Educational Assortative Mating and Female Labor Supply in India

detail.title: Marriage, Education, and Work: Educational Assortative Mating and Female Labor Supply in India
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the impact of educational spousal matching on women's labor force participation (LFP) and time allocation in India, leveraging an instrumental variable approach to correct for endogeneity, and a simple interpretive model. We identify three central patterns: (1) wives in homogamous and hypogamous unions face substantial LFP penalties, typically 10-15 percentage points lower than those in hypergamous unions. (2) Female LFP in non-hypergamous marriages exhibits a pronounced U-shaped relationship with male education: participation initially declines then rebounds as spousal education and household income rise. (3) Hypergamous marriages show a monotonic decline in female LFP with increasing male education. Our results, and the parsimonious model we use to interpret them, underscore how realized match-type-induced patriarchal norms and homeproduction complementarities jointly shape women's labor supply. Because these complementarities also support children's education, policies to raise FLFP under slow-changing norms must reconcile paid work incentives with provisions that protect child human capital formation.

title: Contract-Admissibility Model of Agency 14 in New Vistas Governance

detail.title: Contract-Admissibility Model of Agency 14 in New Vistas Governance
detail.abstract: This article theorizes Agency 14 as the legal-conversion function within the New Vistas constitutional architecture. Unlike a court, public regulator, law firm, policy ministry, or operating agency, Agency 14 holds no adjudicative, executive, pricing, underwriting, or asset-allocation authority. Its task is narrower and more structurally important to translate New Vistas constitutional principles into civilly admissible private-law instruments. These instruments include contract and lease templates, stewardship and transfer agreements, privacy and data-processing clauses, access-control provisions, mediator and adjuster certification standards, bylaw and amendment forms, external-law protocols, legal admissibility forms, and standardized legal language. The paper develops a contractadmissibility framework in which each proposed template is evaluated through nonsubstitutable legal gates. A template is admissible only if it satisfies external civil law, New Vistas constitutional invariants, institutional rail separation, privacy and individual-data ownership, market-rent legality, and domain-specific contractual duties. The model represents a template as a vector of clauses, role assignments, data permissions, payment priorities, market-rent terms, asset-title provisions, and dispute-resolution sequences. It then formalizes Agency 14's function as a legal admissibility test rather than an optimization, enforcement, or policy-making process. The central argument is that Agency 14 prevents three systemic collapses. First, it prevents private covenant from becoming pseudosovereignty by subordinating every agreement to the law of the land and preserving civilcourt authority where required. Second, it prevents community ownership from collapsing into steward ownership or conventional landlordism by distinguishing community title from steward custody, business-transfer value from community-owned assets, and rent-gate residence from later covenant/stewardship conveyance. Third, it prevents market discipline from being displaced by internal price formulas. Resident rent will be market-based, supported by Agency 20 evidence and tested through Agency 21 reverse underwriting; it may not be determined by architectural and accessibility geometry, construction cost, agency fiat, and multiple loan-payment. Double-wide accessible suites may count as two physical slots for planning and underwriting, but billing will have to follow applicable fair-access market rent rather than a geometric double charge. The paper concludes that Agency 14 ensures the legal durability of New Vistas by anchoring its constitutional boundaries in enforceable private law. Through this framework, broad constitutional principles are translated into specific contractual obligations, which in turn establish a legally valid, practical template for civil governance.

High-coordination decentralized public services depend on the continuity of the
local bureaucracy that delivers them. When that continuity breaks without warning,
what gives way and what holds? We study the removal of Brazilian mayors from
office by the electoral courts, which triggers an off-cycle special election whose timing
is governed by the pace of the judicial process and is plausibly exogenous to local
trajectories. Using this shock in a staggered difference-in-differences design across
all 5,570 municipalities, we test whether incentive design shields administrative
routines. Social assistance (CadÚnico/SUAS) offers a rare incentive gradient within
one policy: the Registry Update Rate (TAC) is monetized by the IGD-M, a
performance-based federal transfer; the workforce of the reference centers (CRAS) is
not rewarded; benefit values are federally set. The TAC does not fall after removal,
and the null is precise — drops larger than 1.9 percentage points are ruled out. The
protection carries the signature of the incentive: the TAC declines (−2.6 p.p.) only
where the transfer is marginal. The workforce shows a suggestive ~5% contraction
(exploratory), while rule-bound benefits are not identified. The contrast shifts the
question from diagnosis — does instability degrade services? — to design: which
incentive arrangements cushion the cost.

title: The Wrong Enemy

detail.title: The Wrong Enemy
detail.abstract: This essay argues that the alignment research program is solving a real problem in the wrong order. The agent model of AI risk asks what a system wants; a prior question is whose wanting a system makes executable. Current AI systems are not agents in the catastrophic sense but media: like the ledger and the census before them, they reorganize power not by desiring anything but by removing the friction that previously bounded existing human and institutional desire. Three cases, engagement optimization, autonomous targeting, and the private governance of frontier development, show that the danger is not misuse but successful adoption. The essay's central claim is a sequencing problem: medium-model harms are degrading the institutional capacity, legibility, reversibility, and plurality, on which any future alignment solution will depend, so that technical alignment may succeed in the laboratory and fail in civilization. Scalable oversight, eliciting latent knowledge, and mechanistic interpretability are read as constitutional technologies, and the conditions under which the argument would fail are stated explicitly.

Unveiling Government Disclosures: 
Evidence from Government Transparency on Terrorist Attacks
detail.abstract: This paper examines the trade-offs and consequences of governments' disclosures of private information about public security threats. Using a hand-collected database of government disclosures of foiled terrorist attacks in European countries, we find that governments' disclosure decisions trade off losses for the country's economy with electoral benefits. We document significant reductions in economic activity after the disclosure of foiled terrorist attacks as measured by lower foreign tourist flows to disclosing countries. We further document that government disclosures of foiled terrorist attacks are associated with increased voting intentions for far-right/anti-immigration parties. A battery of additional tests including IV analyses corroborate our inferences. Cross-sectional analyses further show stronger effects on the hospitality industry when media coverage of terrorist attacks is greater or anti-immigration sentiment is stronger in originating countries, and on support for far-right/anti-immigration parties when these factors are stronger in the disclosing country. Overall, our findings provide evidence on the trade-offs shaping government disclosures of public security threats and their impact on economic activity and public opinion.

detail.abstract: Modern monetary systems permit an individual to hold a negative position only through a debt contract, bank credit, or delegated sovereign-deficit authority-each organized through creditor-debtor relations, interest or servicing obligations, and enforceable claims. What no established system, and no major school of economic thought, has adopted is a non-debt negative balance as a universal individual monetary position, bounded not by a creditor's forbearance but by three simultaneous structural constraints: a conservation invariant, lifetime return-to-zero, and a population-uniform capability ceiling. This paper states that construct, proves that conservation holds unconditionally under the accounting axioms, reduces longrun sustainability to a single testable flow inequality (conditional on stated estimation assumptions), and shows that the population-uniform ceiling caps collusion exposure linearly, with no superlinear amplification. It relates the construct precisely to the sectoral-balances identity, to community mutual-credit systems (LETS, WIR), and to demurrage (Gesell), and it ships with an explicit set of predictions a pilot could disconfirm. The organizing question offered for criticism: given these three constraints, does the architecture differ formally from a soft budget constraint, and if it fails, at which constraint does it fail first?

title: Matching with Attributes
affiliations: School of Economics, University of Bristol and University of Cambridge

detail.title: Matching with Attributes
detail.abstract: Firms typically evaluate workers based on their attributes rather than their names, and treat workers with similar attributes similarly. We formalize these natural features through a new property we call density, and recast the classical model of matching with contracts so that in any problem, the set of workers is a finite draw from a rich attribute space. Dense preferences are common in applications and easy to verify. In this environment, simple preference conditions previously known to be necessary but not sufficient become sufficient to guarantee the existence of stable allocations and stable, strategy-proof mechanisms. Thus, attribute-based modelling clarifies which preference restrictions support stable and strategy-proof design, and offers a new lens for revisiting existing matching-withcontracts results.

title: Edgeworth Expansions of Lag-Window-Studentised Statistics under Weak Dependence

detail.title: Edgeworth Expansions of Lag-Window-Studentised Statistics under Weak Dependence
detail.abstract: We derive valid Edgeworth expansions for statistics of the form τn = Ωb−1/2 n Hn(Zn), where Hn is a smooth map, Zn is the scaled empirical mean of a weakly dependent triangular array, and Ωbn is a lag-window estimator of the long-run variance. The resulting signed expansion measure has the triple-series correction structure of Lahiri (2010), with corrections arising jointly from stochastic variance variation, non-Gaussian innovations, and lag-window truncation bias, each contributing at a distinct rate. The paper advances the EE theory for lag-window studentised statistics in three directions: the driving array is row-wise stationary rather than exactly stationary, which is essential for spectral means whose kernel weights depend on the sample size; M-estimators are subsumed via an oracle-reduction argument that eliminates circular dependence on the estimated Hessian and score long-run covariance; and the expansion is established for vector-valued statistics, enabling coverage expansions for chi-squared regions via cancellation of odd-order skewness terms under spherical symmetry. Primitive conditions are verified for three empirically relevant applications under a semiparametric volatility assumption requiring no parametric specification of the volatility dynamics. A central finding is that when the objective gradient process is a martingale difference sequence — as under correctly specified maximum likelihood — the triple-series expansion collapses to a pure n −j/2 series free of lag-window contamination, delivering coverage corrections of order O(n −1 ) rather than the O(b −1 n ) rate under misspecification.

title: The Interaction of Article 102 TFEU and the DMA: Insights from Generative AI Value Chains
affiliations: and University of Siena

detail.title: The Interaction of Article 102 TFEU and the DMA: Insights from Generative AI Value Chains
detail.abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence provides a timely case study for assessing whether existing competition law frameworks are adequately equipped to address exclusionary conduct at the frontier of the digital economy. Article 102 TFEU offers a flexible and conceptually robust legal basis for scrutinising exclusionary practices emerging along the generative-AI value chain. Established CJEU case law on refusal to deal, tying, margin squeeze, and selfpreferencing provides doctrinal tools capable of addressing foreclosure and leveraging risks across both the development and deployment layers. The DMA nonetheless remains well suited to policing newly embedded AI functionalities within the core platform services of designated gatekeepers.

title: Growing Up in Rural Communities: A Thematic Analysis
affiliations: Duke University, University of Oklahoma, University of Oklahoma and University of Oklahoma

detail.title: Growing Up in Rural Communities: A Thematic Analysis
detail.abstract: Early childhood adversity is prevalent in the United States, with rural communities being particularly vulnerable. As rural communities have undergone significant demographic and population shifts in the past few decades, it is crucial to understand specific attributes of rural communities that either promote or inhibit children’s development. The current study used focus group methodology to explore life in rural communities, particularly what it is like growing up in rural towns. Community residents (N = 42) participated in focus groups conducted in five rural towns throughout Oklahoma. Transcripts of the focus group interviews were coded with three broad themes emerging: barriers to well-being, community support for children, and opportunities for growth and revitalization. Findings highlight the challenges of growing up in rural communities, while also acknowledging the areas of strengths. By identifying opportunities for growth and revitalization, this work expands our understanding of specific place-based attributes of rural communities that impact children’s development.

title: Tokenized Transparency: How Efficiency becomes Money

detail.title: Tokenized Transparency: How Efficiency becomes Money
detail.abstract: The world's stablecoins are warehouses. They store value. The SotilityStableToken (SST) is a factory-it creates value. SST is minted not against dollars held in reserve, but against the measurable efficiency surplus generated when an organization integrates Sotility Trust Tech and smart contracts. This paper defines the SST mint mechanism, models its economic implications, and argues that efficiency-backed currency is the most defensible monetary innovation since the gold standard.

title: Anxious Minds, Informative Items: Neuroticism, Risk Aversion, and the Psychometrics of Lottery Choice in Two Indian Samples
affiliations: ,  and Shaheed Sukhdev College of Business Studies (University of Delhi)

detail.title: Anxious Minds, Informative Items: Neuroticism, Risk Aversion, and the Psychometrics of Lottery Choice in Two Indian Samples
detail.abstract: Personality effects on risky choice are usually estimated in Western samples, with little attention to the measurement properties of the choice task itself. We report a two-stage study of neuroticism and lottery risk aversion in India (combined N = 312), combining a preregistered replication with item-response modelling of a five-item hypothetical lottery task. Three results emerge. First, the trait-level association is dependable: neuroticism correlated with risk aversion in both samples (pooled r = 0.25; corrected for measurement error, r = 0.33), and was stable across scoring methods, sample restrictions, and screening for careless responding. Second, neuroticism and intolerance of uncertainty (r = 0.64) predicted risk aversion through a shared negative-affect core; neuroticism carried a small unique increment beyond intolerance of uncertainty, whereas intolerance of uncertainty carried none beyond neuroticism, a caution for using uncertainty scales as stand-alone predictors of economic behaviour. Third, a difficulty-conditional pattern seen under fixed item order did not survive a preregistered randomized-order test; item-response analyses located it in the differential functioning of a single high-information item under fixed order, rather than a difficulty-specific process. Item-level personality effects in such tasks track item information and administration format, so trait-level conclusions should rest on latent or aggregate scores.

title: Duopoly Model with Asymmetric Buyer Distribution
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Duopoly Model with Asymmetric Buyer Distribution
detail.abstract: We introduce asymmetric buyer distribution into a traditional duopoly model to study its impact on equilibria both in price-setting competition and quantity-setting competition. We show that non-negative output constraints become binding when products are close enough substitutes and buyer distribution is asymmetric enough. When these constraints are binding, a rival firm with less than 50% buyer distribution effectively exists the market and monopoly profit is accrued to the surviving firm. Since pricesetting competition is more intense than quantity-setting competition, the market exit occurs with less asymmetric buyer distribution in price-setting competition than in quantity-setting competition. Therefore, the reversal of usual profit ranking can arise in the sense that the surviving firm in price competition earns monopoly profit in price-setting competition while the same firm earns much less duopoly profit in quantity-setting competition. Moreover, three distinct limit equilibria are identified in price-setting competition with perfect substitutes and symmetric buyer distribution. These results highlight an important role played by buyer distribution.

title: Unknown Buyer Distribution between Two Markets, Choice of Price or Quantity in Monopoly
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Unknown Buyer Distribution between Two Markets, Choice of Price or Quantity in Monopoly
detail.abstract: In manufactured durable product markets, sellers regularly launch multiple grades/trims within the same product category to capture a wider range of buyers. In such a situation, a seller needs to evaluate to what extent buyers would be distributed among multiple grades of the product. Suppose a monopolist chooses either price or quantity of all grades simultaneously subject to incomplete information about unknown distribution of buyers. We find that the equilibrium profit is strictly higher in price-setting mode than in quantity-setting mode as long as the buyer distribution remains unknown ex ante. In addition, a price-setting monopolist's profit is unaffected in the presence of uncertainty but a quantitysetting monopolist's profit decreases as the degree of uncertainty rises. In the limit case of maximal uncertainty where one grade capturing 100% share of buyers or 0% share of buyers, a quantitysetting monopolist earns zero expected profit but a price-setting monopolist earns positive expected profit. These results arise because a quantity-setting monopolist's price elasticity approaches to infinity while a price-setting monopolist's price elasticity remains constant.

title: Equity versus Economic Size in the Sixteenth Finance Commission's Horizontal Devolution Formula
affiliations: , University of Delhi and Indian Statistical Institute

detail.title: Equity versus Economic Size in the Sixteenth Finance Commission's Horizontal Devolution Formula
detail.abstract: This paper examines the Sixteenth Finance Commission's horizontal devolution formula for 2026-31. The formula departs from past practice. The one major change is contribution to GDP, a new criterion at 10 per cent weight. The new criterion rewards states with bigger economic size and stands in direct tension with income distance, the dominant equity criterion, which rewards poorer states. The tension between the two criteria reshapes the distribution: transfer-dependent states see their shares erode, while richer states gain. On net, the high-income tier gains 1.19 percentage points and the low-income tier loses 1.38, a reversal of the equalising intent that has historically guided devolution. We construct a proportional-reallocation counterfactual to isolate the new criterion. Taken alone, the new criterion cuts the low-income tier's share by 2.28 points. Coupled with a vertical squeeze from cesses and surcharges, the award tilts, for the first time, toward the states least in need of fiscal support.

title: Social Choice and Market Choice On the Normative Value of Private Contracts in Antitrust Analysis
affiliations: University of Tübingen - Faculty of Law

detail.title: Social Choice and Market Choice On the Normative Value of Private Contracts in Antitrust Analysis
detail.abstract: This article argues that private law contracts have a normative value which warrants stronger recognition in antitrust law. It investigates the function of contracts on markets as a choice mechanism. The analysis, then, traces the legal history of private law contracts, starting in ancient Roman law, over canon law and natural law theory, heeding their influence on continental European law as well as on common law doctrine. This historical viewpoint, in conjunction with an account of the systemic role of contracts in markets, demonstrates how freedom of contract has a normative value which warrants stronger recognition in modern counterfactual antitrust analysis. The normative value lies in the fact that contractual autonomy empowers individuals, including those who constitute numerical minorities, to pursue personal rather than collective ends. From there, the article adopts a critical stance towards modern approaches that seek to expand antitrust doctrine by incorporating societal goals and values outside consumer welfare.

title: Unlocking the Locked: President Trump's 401(k) Reform and the Bitcoin Revolution

detail.title: Unlocking the Locked: President Trump's 401(k) Reform and the Bitcoin Revolution
