detail.abstract: This paper examines the causal effects of temperature deviations from long-term climatic averages on fertility preferences, sexual behavior, and reproductive outcomes among women in India. Combining high-resolution gridded temperature data with individual-level information from the National Family Health Survey, I exploit spatial and temporal variation in temperature to find that colder-than-average years reduce fertility preferences and decrease sexual activity. I find no evidence that temperature affects biological fertility or that changes in sexual behavior are driven by physical exhaustion. Exploring potential mechanisms, I show that although temperature influences several health indicators, these effects do not explain the observed fertility responses. Instead, colder years significantly increase agricultural income, suggesting improved household resources and food security. The findings are consistent with a quantityquality tradeoff, whereby favorable economic conditions encourage greater investment in existing household needs rather than a larger family size.

title: Cross-Asset Momentum Spillover from Commodities to Sector Equities via Granger Causality

detail.title: Cross-Asset Momentum Spillover from Commodities to Sector Equities via Granger Causality
detail.abstract: This paper investigates whether momentum in commodity futures markets contains statistically significant predictive information about subsequent momentum in related sector equity ETFs. Using daily data from January 2010 to May 2026 across five commodity-equity pairs, we apply Granger causality testing, Vector Autoregression (VAR), and Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) analysis to characterise the cross-asset causal structure. We find that all five hypothesised commodity-to-equity spillover relationships are confirmed at the 5% significance level, with Gold→GDX producing the strongest signal (F = 18.90, p < 0.001) and NatGas→XLE the weakest (F = 2.43, p = 0.046). Forecast Error Variance Decomposition reveals that commodity shocks explain 46.4% of GDX momentum variance and 31-37% of XLE momentum variance at short forecast horizons. Rolling Granger tests and Chow structural break analysis reveal that the causal relationships are regime-dependent rather than structurally persistent: near-universal structural breaks are detected at the 2022 energy crisis across all pairs, while COVID-era breaks affect energy and materials pairs but not Gold→GDX. A signal-based long/short backtest confirms regime-conditionality: strategies achieve positive Sharpe ratios during the COVID volatility regime (2020-2022) but deteriorate in the post-energy-crisis period. These findings suggest that commodity-to-equity momentum spillover is a genuine but time-varying causal phenomenon, activated by macro-structural shocks rather than operating as a continuous arbitrage.

title: The Lunous Housing Distress Index: Construction, Validation, and Findings

detail.title: The Lunous Housing Distress Index: Construction, Validation, and Findings

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding. This research was conducted by Lunous, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization.

detail.abstract: The Housing Distress Index (HDI) is a reproducible, county-scale composite measuring structural housingcost conditions-rent-to-income ratio, price-to-income ratio, cost-burdened and severe-cost-burdened shares (the 30%-and 50%-of-income thresholds), and rental vacancy-associated with elevated homelessness outcomes at the population level. We introduce the HDI as a measurement instrument that carries the relationship Colburn and Aldern (2022) document at metropolitan scale, and Glynn, Byrne, and Culhane (2021) at sub-metropolitan (Continuum-of-Care) scale, down to the county resolution at which local measurement and decision-making operate. Signals are pre-registered and assembled into three equal-weighted dimensions: Affordability, Cost Burden, and Availability. A fourth candidate cluster-Economic Vitality, including an income-polarization (inequality) channel-was tested and removed: none of its signals carried independent cross-sectional predictive power, in either direction. Housing cost and supply carry the signal; general economic vitality adds nothing independent at the county scale. Normalization baselines are frozen from the 2010-2019 county discovery panel and shared across vintages, so scores are comparable across years and a county's movement over time re lects actual change against a ixed distribution. Scores are read county-against-county. Validation re-tests Colburn's cost-and-vacancy relationship on the full CBSA panel-using an incomedenominated variant of his original absolute-cost operationalization-and Glynn's cost-burden in lection at the county scale. The cost-burdened share-the fraction of households over the 30%-of-income threshold-proves a stronger cross-sectional predictor than the median cost-to-income ratio (standardized β = 0.230 vs. 0.145): how many households are burdened carries more predictive signal than how burdened the median household is. A Bayesian rolling-origin ablation asks whether affordability also forecasts a county's path over time, and inds that it does not: once a few years of history ix where a county sits, changes in its affordability don't help predict changes in its homelessness. The relationship operates across counties-it is what separates one place from another-while a single county's year-to-year drift is too small, by comparison, to measure. Applied to the 2,967 counties with complete 2024 data, the index discriminates broadly across the 0-100 scale (SD 12.2), and most of that variation is driven by Cost Burden-the steepest dimension, climbing from a mean of 37 in the lowest composite quartile to 80 in the highest. We then screen 393 active CoCs for bright spots: places with a sustained, multi-year decline in homelessness that shows no sign of having come from displacing vulnerable residents rather than housing them. The decline is tracked through point-in-time counts-single-night, undercounted snapshots, reliable more as a direction of travel than an exact level. Only 3 CoCs qualify; 14 more are set aside for displacement review. A sustained decline without signs of displacement is rare. All artifacts are SHA-256 frozen and publicly reproducible through a curated replication repository. The index measures one thing: how hard housing conditions push an entire community toward homelessness. Who actually falls into homelessness under that pressure is a separate question-shaped by personal vulnerability such as mental illness or addiction, by the depth of entrenched disadvantage, and by policy exclusions that fall hardest on particular groups-and one this paper does not take up. That pressure is harder to see than the individual stories, and it is what this index measures.

title: Kamikaze Drones and Neo-Warfare: Evolution, Doctrine and Proliferation of Iranian Drones in Contemporary Armed Conflicts

detail.abstract:
This paper examines the evolution of drone warfare through the lens of Iran's kamikaze drone doctrine, focusing on the Shahed-136 loitering munition and its proliferation in contemporary armed conflicts. It argues that the shift from costly, precision-oriented UAVs such as the U.S. MQ-9 Reaper to cheap, mass-producible "kamikaze" or "suicide" drones represents a structural transformation in the economics and conduct of war, prioritising affordability, scalability, and expendability over technological sophistication.

Tracing three phases in the evolution of drone warfare, the paper situates Iran's doctrine as a product of sanctions-driven necessity that has enabled asymmetric warfare against technologically superior adversaries. It further explores the horizontal and vertical proliferation of this technology to state actors such as Russia, via the Geran-2 variant, and non-state actors including the Houthis and Hezbollah, as well as the reverse proliferation reflected in the United States' development of the LUCAS drone system. Finally, the paper assesses the legal and ethical challenges these systems pose to International Humanitarian Law, particularly regarding the principles of distinction, proportionality, and accountability. It concludes that Iran's drone doctrine reflects the emergence of a broader model of "neo-warfare," characterised by decentralisation, economic asymmetry, and sustained low-intensity remote attacks that blur the line between war and peace.

detail.abstract: Biometric recognition has become a dominant mechanism for identification and access control across consumer, enterprise, government, and forensic domains. This article provides a comprehensive survey of the use of biometrics for security and the corresponding misuse cases, security issues, and mitigation strategies. We review the generic biometric pipeline and its performance metrics, compare thirteen physiological and behavioral modalities, and analyze the established eight-point attack model alongside emerging threats driven by generative artificial intelligence, including deepfakes, voice cloning, face morphing, and synthetic master-prints. We discuss the advantages of biometrics for security systems and cyber-forensic investigations, as well as their limitations, demographic-bias concerns, and the legal landscape (GDPR, HIPAA, BIPA, the EU AI Act, and India's DPDP Act). Three landmark data breaches and several 2022-2025 incidents are examined as forensic case studies. Finally, we survey defensesmultimodal fusion, presentation attack detection, multi-factor authentication, biometric cryptosystems, cancelable biometrics, advanced template protection, and on-device, standards-aligned architectures (ISO/IEC 30107 and 24745, NIST testing, and FIDO2). The synthesis is intended to guide researchers, practitioners, and policymakers toward the effective and responsible use of biometrics.

title:
Accountability without Authority:
Why Governance Systems Fail despite Assigned Responsibility

detail.title:
Accountability without Authority:
Why Governance Systems Fail despite Assigned Responsibility
detail.abstract: Governance scholarship has traditionally treated accountability assignment as a central mechanism through which responsible action is expected to occur. This paper argues that accountability assignment and intervention authority are analytically distinct governance properties and that their separation is a recurring contributor to governance failure. Drawing on the Decision-Execution Layer Model (DLM) and on empirical evidence from thirty cross-sector governance failure cases, this paper develops that argument through three analytical contributions. The paper introduces the Accountability-Authority Matrix, a two-dimensional framework classifying governance systems by the presence or absence of accountability assignment and intervention authority. Four configurations are identified: Governance Capacity, Accountability Without Authority, Authority Without Accountability, and Governance Vacuum. Detailed case analysis of five governance failures provides evidence consistent with the proposition that the accountability-authority separation is observable across aviation, finance, healthcare, technology, and AI deployment contexts. The paper further argues that escalation architecture functions as the critical bridging mechanism between accountability assignment and intervention authority: without a functional escalation pathway, accountability cannot be converted into action regardless of how clearly responsibility is assigned. While aspects of this separation have been explored in the principal-agent, delegation, and regulatory capacity literatures, the existing scholarship has not systematically integrated these concepts into a governance execution framework applicable across sectors. This paper proposes an integrated governance execution framework that brings these concepts together. The central implication for governance design is that accountability frameworks must be accompanied by explicit authority designation and functional escalation architecture to produce governance outcomes. Accountability was present. The authority to convert it into action was not.

title: Beyond Academics: The Long-Term Effects of Early Childhood Education on Subjective Well-being in China

detail.title: Beyond Academics: The Long-Term Effects of Early Childhood Education on Subjective Well-being in China
detail.abstract: Early childhood education (ECE) has long been recognized as a foundation for lifelong development, yet its impact on adult subjective well-being remains underexplored, particularly in non-WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic) contexts such as China. This study examines the long-term associations between ECE and adult well-being outcomes using data from the 2018 China Family Panel Studies. Propensity Score Matching was used alongside various robustness checks to address selection bias. The results show that ECE participation is significantly associated with lower levels of depression and reductions in the overall composite negative well-being index. On the other hand, no significant effects were observed for positive well-being outcomes. These findings highlight ECE's potential as a buffer against adverse psychological outcomes in adulthood and highlight the importance of integrating well-being measures into Chinese education policies.

title: The Art of Strategic Noise: When to Poison a Data Science Contest?
affiliations: Fudan, Fudan University - School of Management, School of Economics, Peking Univeristy and Fudan University

detail.title: The Art of Strategic Noise: When to Poison a Data Science Contest?
detail.abstract: Data science contests enable seekers to crowdsource predictive and algorithmic solutions from heterogeneous solvers, but releasing training data often raises the need to protect sensitive information, such as user-side privacy and firm-side proprietary business information. A common response is to poison the released data by injecting noise. Prior work predominantly treats such poisoning as a data-protection necessity that inherently degrades data utility. We reconceptualize data poisoning as a strategic contest-design lever to manage solvers' incentives. We develop a model wherein a seeker chooses the noise scale and two heterogeneous solvers choose their effort. Data poisoning generates a fundamental tradeoff: it worsens data quality but levels the playing field and stimulates effort. We establish a moderate-asymmetry principle: poisoning is optimal only when solvers' expertise asymmetry is moderate-large enough to warrant leveling the playing field, but not so large that the requisite noise destroys the data's intrinsic value. Furthermore, we identify a complementarity between data poisoning and prize design. Strategically injecting noise restores competitive pressure, optimally inducing the seeker to augment the prize purse and potentially achieving a Pareto improvement that strictly benefits all parties. Finally, extending the analysis to a multi-solver environment reveals that optimal poisoning depends crucially on expertise skewness in addition to the dispersion. Overall, our results recast data poisoning from a defensive data-protection instrument into a proactive economic design choice.

title: Three Nulls, One Verdict: Calibrating the eforensics Election-Fraud Model Against Two Decades of Korean Elections
affiliations: University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign

detail.title: Three Nulls, One Verdict: Calibrating the eforensics Election-Fraud Model Against Two Decades of Korean Elections
detail.abstract: Bayesian finite-mixture election-forensics models in the tradition of Mebane [2016] classify votecounting units as clean or fraudulent from aggregate turnout and vote-share data alone, without independent evidence of manipulation. We evaluate the eforensics quasi-binomial-logistic (qbl) model against 20 years of Korean elections (2002-2025), fitting 576 separate model runs spanning general and presidential elections, two aggregation levels, up to five vote-counting channels, both directions of leader coding, and, critically, two independently constructed fraud-free synthetic controls calibrated to match each real dataset's turnout and vote-share marginals without any fraud-generating mechanism. We find that the model reports substantial "fraud" (5-29% of units, into the millions of "fraudulent" votes) on data that is fraud-free by construction; that real-data fraud-share estimates correlate at r ≈ 0.96 with their fraud-free null counterparts across 58 paired cells under each leader coding; that the model's largest real-data estimates fall on presidential elections held before Korea had early voting or any fraud allegations (2002-2012), exceeding what it reports for the actually contested 2020 election; and that recoding the model to test fraud in the opposite (conservative-favoring) direction reproduces the identical pathology across the complete 11-election grid, with the Democratic-coded estimate exceeding the conservative-coded estimate in most, but not all, cells, an asymmetry itself matched by fraud-free nulls rather than indicating real fraud in either direction. A direct comparison of short against long MCMC chains on a matched subsample shows convergence failure and fraud-share estimates are statistically indistinguishable between settings, indicating the non-convergence pervasive in this corpus is not an artifact of insufficient sampling. We conclude that the model's output depends on the shape of the (turnout, vote-share) distribution, not on fraud, and that this failure is not fixable by post-hoc recalibration, since recalibrating for validity would remove essentially all detected signal in the corpus.

title: Involuntary Job Separation and Entry into Elementary Occupations among Older Korean Wage Workers: The Gendered Vanishing Penalty
affiliations: Korea Employment Information Service, Korea University and Korea Polytechnics

detail.title: Involuntary Job Separation and Entry into Elementary Occupations among Older Korean Wage Workers: The Gendered Vanishing Penalty
detail.abstract: Using waves 1–10 of the Korean Longitudinal Study of Ageing (KLoSA, 2006–2024), we estimate how involuntary job separation affects the occupational destination of wage workers aged 45 and over. From separation events anchored to the previous-wave job, we analyze 1,226 separations with observed outcomes (391 involuntary, 835 voluntary), combining entropy balancing with covariate-adjusted weighted logistic regression and person-clustered bootstrap inference (B=5,000). At age 50, involuntary separation raises the odds of re-employment in an elementary occupation by a factor of 2.40 (95% CI [1.12, 5.84], p=0.028). Because this outcome conditions on re-employment, identification is anchored in a co-primary multinomial decomposition over all separators: involuntary separation raises the relative risk of elementary entry (RRR 2.14, p=0.035) with no effect on exit from wage employment (p=0.27) — the penalty operates through allocation, not withdrawal. Sex-stratified Lee (2009) bounds show the female penalty survives worst-case selection (bounds: +0.10 to +0.25); pooled bounds straddle zero only by averaging in the null male stratum. Excluding workers already in elementary jobs strengthens the effect (OR 3.52, p=0.014). The penalty differs sharply by sex in level — large for women, statistically insignificant for men (pooled test p=0.016) — and fades with age for women (vanishing near 62; ridge-stabilized OR 3.3 (95% CI [1.5, 8.0])); whether the fade itself differs by sex is suggestive (joint p=0.096). Elementary occupations form an absorbing floor whose gate opens differently by sex, implying separation-reason-blind support is inefficient and policy should differentiate by gender while upgrading absorbing-sector job quality.

title: High-Performance Programming Models and Reproducibility for Financial AI on GPUs: A Mojo-Centered Survey
affiliations: Department of Computer Science, School of Engineering & Computer Science, Baylor University

detail.title: High-Performance Programming Models and Reproducibility for Financial AI on GPUs: A Mojo-Centered Survey
detail.abstract: Financial artificial intelligence, spanning deep forecasting, reinforcement learning for execution and hedging, generative scenario models, and large Monte Carlo risk engines, is increasingly limited by the throughput, energy, and latency of the graphics processing unit (GPU) rather than by model design. Practitioners face a persistent gap between productivity, offered by Python frameworks such as PyTorch, and performance, offered by handwritten CUDA C. This survey organizes the landscape of high-performance GPU programming models for financial AI along that productivity-to-performance axis. It runs from low-level CUDA, through Python frameworks (PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX) and just-in-time or domain-specific compilers (Numba, Triton, CuPy), to Mojo, a recent Python superset that compiles through a multi-level compiler intermediate representation (MLIR) and targets the GPU directly. Alongside performance, we give equal weight to a second axis the financial AI literature has under-served: reproducibility, both numerical (bitwise determinism) and empirical (fair, precision-matched benchmarking). A central theme is that reproducibility separates these programming models as sharply as speed does. Because Mojo exposes the exact floating-point operation order, it can guarantee bitwise-identical results, a guarantee that CUDA shares but that the dominant tensor frameworks do not provide by default. Mojo thus reaches the productive end of the axis without giving up the numerical control that regulated finance requires. Following an explicit review protocol over roughly ninety primary sources, we contribute a taxonomy of programming models, a mapping of financial AI workloads to their GPU compute profiles, a reproducibility framework with formal determinism guarantees, and an original empirical case study that evaluates Mojo against handwritten CUDA and PyTorch on five financial workloads under matched numerics. Across these workloads Mojo matches CUDA on streaming kernels at bitwise-identical results and trails it on two stateful kernels, while running an order of magnitude or more faster than idiomatic PyTorch. We close with open challenges for reproducible, high-performance financial AI.

title: All Explanations are Wrong, But Many Are Useful: Exploring the Rashomon Explanation Set with Large Language Models
affiliations: Georgia Institute of Technology - IT Management Area

detail.title: All Explanations are Wrong, But Many Are Useful: Exploring the Rashomon Explanation Set with Large Language Models
detail.abstract: Explaining machine-learning models is increasingly important for decision-making and consumer trust, yet it is widely believed to come at a cost: existing Explainable AI (XAI) methods suffer from a persistent accuracy-explainability trade-off. We argue that this trade-off is not fundamental, but rather an artifact of treating explanation and prediction as two separate objectives; when the two are properly coupled, they become complementary, such that equipping a model to explain itself improves, rather than degrades, its predictive accuracy. Realizing this benefit, however, requires overcoming three limitations of existing XAI methods: (1) no single explanation remains valid under distribution shift; (2) scalar attributions, such as SHAP, cannot capture conditional or nonlinear relationships; and (3) explanations are disconnected from the predictions they inform. We therefore introduce the Rashomon Explanation paradigm for building a set of faithful, predictionguiding explanations rather than a single one, and we prove that this set is generally non-empty and that the fidelity of these explanations bounds the performance of the models they guide. To explore the set of Rashomon Explanation, motivated by the organizational theories of sensemaking and double-loop learning, we propose RashomonLLM, an Explanation-Prediction-Reflection LLM agentic workflow that generates the explanation set in natural language by iteratively aligning the explanation with the prediction. We prove that under explicit conditions, RashomonLLM converges and recovers the full Rashomon Explanation set. Empirically, across three applications of customer-churn classification, clinical survival regression, and industrial clickthrough prediction on large-scale logs from Kuaishou's live-streaming platform, RashomonLLM significantly outperforms state-of-the-art prediction and XAI baselines on both accuracy and explanation quality, and surpasses strong specialized deep CTR models. Furthermore, ablation, robustness, and calibration analyses confirm that this accuracy gain is achieved by equipping the model to explain itself and is driven by explanation fidelity, and that it persists across distribution shifts, temporal splits, and random seeds. As a result, our framework enables organizations to advance business performance and lay the groundwork for consumer trust at the same time.

detail.title: From Direct Mail to Bonded Warehousing: Building a Coherent Legal and Institutional Framework for Cross-Border B2C E-Commerce in Uzbekistan Declaration of Interest
detail.abstract:
This policy brief examines the legal and institutional framework for cross-border B2C e-commerce in Uzbekistan, with a focus on the transition from direct international delivery and fragmented warehousing arrangements toward a coherent bonded warehouse-based model. The rapid growth of online platforms and demand for imported goods has increased the importance of efficient customs, logistics, and fulfillment systems. However, Uzbekistan’s current framework still relies on instruments originally designed for bulk trade, storage, re-export, and courier delivery, rather than high-volume digital retail flows linked to final consumers.

The brief argues that Uzbekistan already has partial legal foundations for a bonded warehouse-type model, but lacks a dedicated regime tailored to e-commerce needs, including pre-importation, digital processing, unit-level release, online fulfillment, returns, re-export, and integrated data exchange. The main barriers are not only legal, but also institutional and economic, including high guarantee requirements, licensing burdens, capital lock-in, retail restrictions, and weak coordination between customs, tax, logistics, and e-commerce frameworks.

Drawing on international experience, the paper shows that effective bonded warehouse regimes operate as integrated systems combining legal clarity, operator accreditation, simplified release procedures, digital data exchange, transparency, traceability, and safeguards against abuse. The brief proposes a sequenced reform approach for Uzbekistan aimed at improving logistics efficiency, strengthening compliance, enhancing liquidity, increasing fiscal visibility, and supporting a more competitive cross-border e-commerce ecosystem.

detail.abstract:
This policy brief examines the need for a dedicated bonded warehouse regime for cross-border e-commerce in Uzbekistan. The current system relies mainly on direct international mail and fragmented customs procedures. As online trade expands, this model creates delays, raises logistics costs, increases pressure on customs, and limits transparency.

The brief assesses three possible scenarios: maintaining the current system, introducing a limited pilot regime, and moving to full-scale implementation. The analysis suggests that a bonded warehouse model would allow goods to be imported in bulk, stored under customs control, and cleared at the unit level when sold to final consumers. This could shorten delivery times, reduce administrative costs, improve compliance, and support the growth of local marketplaces and SMEs.

The brief concludes that a dedicated e-commerce bonded warehouse regime should be treated as more than a technical customs reform. It can become an important part of Uzbekistan’s digital trade infrastructure, help formalize cross-border e-commerce flows, and strengthen the country’s potential as a regional logistics hub.

detail.title: Deconstructing the Machine Learning Value Chain
detail.abstract: This essay offers a materialist analysis of machine learning in the form of a critical intervention that deconstructs the value chain of this technological paradigm. It is structured around three interrelated concepts that provide a deeper understanding of the political economy of machine learning. First is innovation realism: the idea that venture capital is the best or only way to support innovation, and alternative approaches are inferior or impossible. Second is cheap data: the structural contradiction that, despite data being the most essential part of technological capitalism, it is also the most undervalued and taken for granted. Third is the perpetual value machine: the pursuit by capital to create technologies that capture an infinite amount of surplus value without needing to rely on any additional human labor to produce that value.

title: AI-Assisted Urban Governance: Deployment Insights from a Multi-Model Aerial Detection System Across Ten Chinese Cities

detail.title: AI-Assisted Urban Governance: Deployment Insights from a Multi-Model Aerial Detection System Across Ten Chinese Cities

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Jiaheng Liu holds a degree in Computer Science from the University of New South Wales (UNSW). He previously worked in the ICT division of a Huawei research institute, where he worked on Ascend AI accelerators and applied AI systems. He is currently the large-model and AI lead at Huati Technology Co., Ltd., where he leads the multi-model aerial recognition and urban-governance platform described in this paper — including its detection pipeline, vision-language verification cascade, and data-flywheel components. declarations.ethicsApproval: This study analyzes aerial video of public urban traffic and infrastructure scenes for governance monitoring. It does not involve human subjects, patients, or clinical experiments, and therefore did not require ethics-board approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by Huati Technology Co., Ltd. No external funding was received.

detail.abstract:
Municipal authorities increasingly turn to unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to monitor urban violations — illegal parking, occupied roadways, infrastructure defects, and safety hazards — across areas too large for fixed cameras or on-foot inspection to cover. Yet moving from a promising demonstration to a system that municipal operators trust in daily governance work exposes problems that laboratory benchmarks never surface: how to avoid falsely citing a driver who is merely waiting at a red light, how to keep an AI verifier from rubber-stamping its own detector's mistakes, and how to keep recognition accuracy from collapsing when operators ask the system to watch for many things at once.

This paper reports on a multi-model aerial detection system deployed for urban-governance tasks across ten Chinese cities over fourteen months. Rather than presenting a single algorithm, we distill five **design principles** that emerged from deployment and that we believe generalize to any jurisdiction adopting AI-assisted aerial monitoring: (1) inferring an unobservable cause from synchronized behavior; (2) preventing camera-motion artifacts from corrupting evidence; (3) calibrating de-duplication to the timing of aerial revisits; (4) separating perception from judgment to keep AI errors from compounding; and (5) limiting how many rules an AI verifier handles at once. On 45 hours of annotated municipal footage the deployed system reaches 0.88 accuracy at a 0.03 false-positive rate, and it operates on novel scene types without site-specific retraining. We close with governance and policy implications: what these principles imply for procurement, for fairness and accountability in automated enforcement, and for the human-oversight structures that make AI-assisted governance defensible.

title:
Opt-In is Not Consent

detail.abstract:
Opting in to a feature is not blanket permission for every later use of the data. A user taps “enable” so a map can start in the right place, turns on memory so an assistant remembers preferences, or uploads a file so an artificial intelligence (AI) tool can summarize it. Those choices help the product work. They also can be stretched to justify longer retention, commercial processing, AI training, reverse searches, and disclosure when a subpoena, a warrant, a court order, or an emergency disclosure request arrives. The mismatch is the consent gap. 

In Chatrie v. United States, the Supreme Court held that police conducted a Fourth Amendment search when they obtained Google Location History through a geofence warrant - a warrant asking a provider to identify devices in a defined area during a defined time. The data covered only a limited period, was held by a third-party technology company, and came from a feature the user enabled. That holding directly affects geofence warrants. It also exposes a broader design problem for technology companies and artificial intelligence platforms. 

Consent drift describes the mechanism: permission given for one practical purpose expands over time to cover later uses the user may not have understood. The response proposed here is lawful access by design: companies decide before launch what sensitive data to collect, how long to keep it, how to store it, when to train on it, and how to respond if the government later seeks the data. Drawing on Chatrie, Carpenter, California digital privacy cases, the California Electronic Communications Privacy Act (CalECPA), the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA), the California Privacy Rights Act (CPRA), California Privacy Protection Agency (CPPA) risk assessment and automated decisionmaking technology (ADMT) regulations, Federal Trade Commission (FTC) artificial consent enforcement, and established privacy and AI risk management frameworks, the analysis offers three concrete tools: purpose-specific notice, legal-process matrices, and Government Access Impact Assessments. 

The practical argument is simple: companies should decide what sensitive data to collect, how long to keep it, and how they will respond to subpoenas, warrants, court orders, and emergency disclosure requests before one arrives.

detail.abstract: One of the biggest technological trends of the 21st century is rapid cloudification of advanced manufacturing. This paper will review the cloud-based applications that are transforming reliability in today's modern manufacturing environments and analyze them in the context of the author's current industry experience in enterprise integration architecture, designing solutions across Microsoft Azure and AWS, and personal experience in large-scale digital transformation programs within the chemical manufacturing sector. title: BOT (Built On Trust): An AI-supported Mediation System for Participatory Spatial Planning in German-speaking Europe

detail.title: BOT (Built On Trust): An AI-supported Mediation System for Participatory Spatial Planning in German-speaking Europe
detail.abstract: Growing complexity in urban planning processes confronts municipal planning offices with mounting methodological challenges: integrating data across heterogeneous systems, processing digital citizen participation, and producing legally sound documentation of balancing-of-interests decisions under German planning law (BauGB) frequently exceed the personnel capacity of mid-sized municipalities. This concept paper introduces BOT, an AI-supported mediation system that combines GIS-based spatial analysis, structured evaluation of citizen participation, and planning-law balancing logic within one integrated workflow. The conceptual core of the artifact is a reframing move: drawing on Actor-Network Theory (Latour) and using autopoietic systems theory (Maturana/Varela) as a reference point, the individual parcel or vacant lot is modeled as an active network actor that signals demand and co-initiates planning processes within a rule-of-law-bounded degree-of-automation model. The artifact is currently in the concept and design phase; this paper documents problem identification, theoretical grounding, conceptual design, and an ex ante evaluation based on structured expert criteria. The findings indicate that BOT addresses a documented gap in the planning-software ecosystem of the German-speaking region (Germany, Austria, Switzerland) and can be positioned as a scalable SaaS solution for municipalities.

title: The Empty Learner Model: Classifying Artificial Intelligence in Education by Epistemic Warrant
affiliations: UWE Bristol, Department of Computer Science

No products of Explore Learning are evaluated in this review; the company appears only as a declared aﬃliation. The analysis and conclusions are the author’s own.

detail.abstract: The evidence on artificial intelligence in education contradicts itself: meta-analyses report large positive effects on achievement while randomised experiments show the same underlying technology leaving learners worse off than if they had never used it. This paper argues that the contradiction is categorical before it is empirical, because “AI in education” aggregates systems that share an interface and little of pedagogical substance, and proposes a framework that classifies systems by epistemic warrant: the depth of the learner model (five cumulative levels, from a within-session trace to a calibrated estimate of supported and independent capability), the adaptation mechanism (content production, learner-state estimation, and pedagogical decision policy, coded separately), the locus of agency (per function, with the withdrawal of assistance weighted most), and evidential maturity (grade of evidence and direction of durable outcome, recorded separately and never merged). Each dimension is derived from established results in the learning sciences rather than induced from outcome data. Read through the framework, the field’s landmark evidence is consistent with a danger configuration, where generative adaptation meets a shallow learner model and no evidence of durable benefit, and with a historical slide of deployed systems toward that configuration. Both claims are stated as falsifiable hypotheses, five in all, alongside five design and procurement propositions. A companion study applying the framework’s codebook to the corpus with independent raters is in preparation.

title: Free First vs. Trial First: Onboarding Design and Premium Discovery in Freemium Services
affiliations: Arizona State University (ASU) - W.P. Carey School of Business, , Southwestern University of Finance and Economics (SWUFE), The Hong Kong Polytechnic University and School of Computing and Artificial lntelligence

detail.title: Free First vs. Trial First: Onboarding Design and Premium Discovery in Freemium Services
detail.abstract: Freemium firms often choose between a free first approach, where new users begin in the basic version, and a trial first approach, where onboarding guides users into a free premium trial. We argue that this choice determines who bears the cost of discovering premium value. Because premium features are experience goods, users must reach and experience premium before they can judge its worth, yet users left in a free first flow rarely seek it out on their own. We study a natural experiment at a large image-editing platform, where an unexpected glitch shifted desktop onboarding from the normal trial first flow to a free first flow for 48 hours while the free trial remained available elsewhere. Using a difference-indifferences design on 174,159 new users, we estimate that free first lowers subscription by 42%. Clickstream evidence further shows that free first works by keeping users from reaching premium at all, not by changing how they evaluate it afterward. The effect persists in lower yearly-plan adoption and two-year spending, and refund patterns suggest that trial first expands conversion without diluting subscriber quality. The disadvantage of free first is larger where users face greater uncertainty or exploration frictions and disappears for high-intent organic-search users, a gradient consistent with a discovery-cost mechanism rather than a mechanical loss of a visible entry point.

title: Between Red and Blue Oceans: Strategic Innovation Distance, Competitive Congestion, and US Firm Performance - A Large-Sample Empirical Analysis of Heuristic Mis-specification

detail.title: Between Red and Blue Oceans: Strategic Innovation Distance, Competitive Congestion, and US Firm Performance - A Large-Sample Empirical Analysis of Heuristic Mis-specification

detail.abstract: This paper investigates whether Blue Ocean strategy components improve firm performance. Existing literature lacks an evaluation of the interplay between innovation novelty (λ) and competitive congestion (cong) (a theoretical gap), the measurement of strategic innovation distance within large, representative datasets (a methodological gap), and the alignment between 'Blue Ocean' management heuristics and actual market dynamics across multi-dimensional performance outcomes. We address these gaps by introducing a ratio λ / (cong+1), extracting Strategic Innovation Distance, Competitive Congestion and uncertainty metrics from a large-scale dataset of corporate SEC 10-K filings for the all-firm group (N = 68,806 firm-year observations) and S&P 500 group (N = 5,515), using lexicographical analysis and local LLM methods (while controlling for HHI, Operating Profit Margin, and R&D intensity) and using structured 5x5 and 3x3 performance scenario matrices. The empirical results demonstrate that as the (λ / (cong+1)) ratio increases, firm performance (ROA) tends to grow, with a fallback at the 7th decile and a decline in the 10th decile. The decline was persistent within the lower-revenue cohort (Q2) and mid-sized firm groups (size Q2–Q3). The matrix indicates that in the S&P 500 and the top revenue quartile (Q4) of the all-firm group, profitability is positively moderated by the confluence of strategic novelty and moderate-to-high competitive congestion. Conversely, in the lower-revenue (Q1 and Q2) and smaller firm size (Q1- Q3) quartiles, strategic novelty exerts a negative effect on size and leverage-adjusted ROA. The hypothesis that the profitability of radical strategic differentiation is negatively moderated by the absence of competitive congestion is supported.

title: Interdisciplinary Barriers in the Formation of Smart Cities: From Architecture to Cybersecurity

detail.title: Interdisciplinary Barriers in the Formation of Smart Cities: From Architecture to Cybersecurity
detail.abstract: The concept of Smart City has emerged as a multidimensional framework that integrates architecture, engineering, information technology, urban planning, and governance to enhance the quality of urban life. However, the implementation of Smart City projects encounters significant interdisciplinary barriers. This paper examines the challenges that arise at the intersection of architecture, infrastructure development, information and communication technologies (ICT), and cybersecurity. Particular attention is given to issues of interoperability between architectural and digital systems, data management and privacy concerns, as well as the lack of unified standards that can align diverse professional fields. Furthermore, the article highlights the organizational and social barriers that hinder effective collaboration among architects, urban planners, IT specialists, and policymakers. The findings indicate that successful Smart City integration requires not only technological solutions but also interdisciplinary dialogue, standardization of processes, and sustainable governance models. By addressing these barriers, cities can build a resilient foundation for future urban development, ensuring efficiency, security, and inclusivity.

title: Costless Degradation, Versioning and Competition
affiliations: Emory University - Goizueta Business School

detail.title: Costless Degradation, Versioning and Competition
detail.abstract:
A digital-product firm makes two decisions that are usually studied as one: how good a product to
develop, and how many versions of it to sell. Two properties of information goods bear on both
decisions, and prior work treats them in isolation. A firm can degrade its developed product into
lower-quality versions at essentially no cost, so its quality is itself a choice. And consumers often lack
free disposal: unwanted features carry usage costs, so the fullest version is not best for everyone. In
our duopoly each firm chooses, through a research and development (R&D) cost, the highest quality it
develops; the firms then compete menu against menu. Within the class of product lines we analyze,
the shape of consumer utility alone settles the structure of competition: the firms never develop the
same top quality; their lines never overlap; prices are set on the gap between the lines; and, with
two lines offered, the higher screens through an increasing price menu while the lower sells every
version at one price, customers picking what they want. Once development is endogenized under a
quadratic usage cost, two-sided versioning does not survive in the configurations we characterize:
depending on R&D costs and taste concentration, one firm versions while the other sells a single
product. At the free-disposal benchmark neither firm versions in a covered market. The model nests
free disposal, monopoly, and single-product competition as special cases, recovering their results
within one framework and bringing a fragmented versioning literature into one perspective.

title: The Fintech-Forensics Paradox: Evaluating Proportionality in Bank Account Freezes Against Bona Fide Merchants Under the BNSS, 2023

detail.title: The Fintech-Forensics Paradox: Evaluating Proportionality in Bank Account Freezes Against Bona Fide Merchants Under the BNSS, 2023
detail.abstract: As India solidifies its position as a global leader in real-time digital payments, the friction between technological commerce and traditional criminal investigation has reached a critical juncture. Law enforcement agencies, in their pursuit of cyber-fraudsters, frequently invoke Section 106 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) the successor to Section 102 of the CrPC to execute blanket debit freezes on bank accounts. A pressing regulatory paradox emerges when defrauded funds are transferred to bona fide merchants as consideration for everyday goods, leading to the freezing of their entire operational accounts. This paper critically examines the legality of such blanket freezing orders in the BNSS era. Relying on the constitutional Doctrine of Proportionality and the ratio laid down in Sri Sai Wines v. State of Andhra Pradesh, this paper argues that disproportionate freezes violate Article 19(1)(g) and Article 300A of the Constitution. It proposes a transition from archaic "blanket freezes" to technology-driven "partial liens" and mandates statutory post-freeze intimation, balancing cyber forensics with the ease of doing business.

title: Responsible Artificial Intelligence Adoption and Future Business Readiness in Hospitality and Tourism in the USA

detail.title: Responsible Artificial Intelligence Adoption and Future Business Readiness in Hospitality and Tourism in the USA
detail.abstract: Hospitality and tourism in the United States is entering an AI-intensive phase in which hotels, airlines, destination marketing organizations, travel agencies, restaurants, event venues and visitor attractions increasingly rely on intelligent automation, predictive analytics, conversational agents and AI-augmented decision systems. These technologies can improve demand forecasting, revenue management, guest personalization, workforce scheduling, service recovery, fraud detection and destination planning. However, the same technologies also intensify ethical, legal and strategic risks associated with privacy, biased recommendations, algorithmic price discrimination, opaque automated decisions, cyber exposure, employee displacement and loss of human-centered service quality. This article develops a responsible AI adoption and futurereadiness framework for hospitality and tourism organizations in the USA. Using a conceptual research design grounded in academic literature, NIST AI Risk Management Framework principles, tourism-sector AI policy discussions, and U.S. consumer protection expectations, the article argues that future readiness depends not only on technical adoption but also on governance maturity, workforce capability, data stewardship, customer trust, and continuous ethical assurance. The proposed Responsible AI Hospitality and Tourism Readiness Framework integrate seven dimensions: strategic value alignment, data and technology readiness, people and culture, ethical design, governance and compliance, operating model maturity, and performance learning. The study concludes that responsible AI can become a source of sustainable competitive advantage when it is implemented through transparent, human-supervised, and riskbased systems rather than as a purely cost-reduction tool.

title: Deployment Context Risk Review (DCRR) A Prospective Governance Documentation Standard for AI-Supported Justice Environments Conceptual Foundations, Scope, and Implications for AI Governance

detail.title: Deployment Context Risk Review (DCRR) A Prospective Governance Documentation Standard for AI-Supported Justice Environments Conceptual Foundations, Scope, and Implications for AI Governance
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into justice-sector operations to support decision-making across correctional institutions, courts, probation and parole agencies, community supervision programs, and law enforcement organizations. Contemporary AI governance frameworks have significantly advanced responsible deployment by emphasizing transparency, accountability, human oversight, lifecycle risk management, documentation, and organizational governance (European Commission, 2024; National Institute of Standards and Technology [NIST], 2023; Organizations for Economic Co-operation and Development [OECD], 2019; UNESCO, 2021). While these frameworks have strengthened governance of AI systems, comparatively less attention has been devoted to documenting the operational decision environments into which those systems are deployed. This paper introduces Deployment Context Risk Review (DCRR) as a prospective governance documentation standard designed to characterize the operational decision environment before AI-supported technologies become part of routine institutional practice. Rather than evaluating algorithmic performance, validating technical systems, or assessing regulatory compliance, DCRR establishes a contemporaneous governance baseline describing the organizational context in which AI-supported information first becomes institutional decision-making. The framework documents characteristics of the operational environment including institutional authority, practitioner discretion, organizational conditions, and anticipated decision pathways without prescribing operational behavior or evaluating technological capability. The paper further argues that prospective governance documentation represents a distinct governance function that complements existing AI governance frameworks by addressing a different analytical question: not whether an AI system is technically prepared for deployment, but whether the operational decision environment surrounding its use has been systematically documented. By distinguishing governance documentation from technical assessment and operational context from technological performance, DCRR contributes to a broader understanding of AI governance that includes both technological systems and the organizational environments in which institutional decisions ultimately occur.

title: Guidelines to Preventing AI Hallucinations in MS Fabric
affiliations: and Independent

detail.title: Guidelines to Preventing AI Hallucinations in MS Fabric
detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) hallucinations-fluent but incorrect or ungrounded outputs generated by large language models-pose a significant barrier to the reliable adoption of generative AI in enterprise environments. In Microsoft Fabric, where Copilot interacts directly with organizational data and analytical workflows, hallucinations can lead to fabricated values, inaccurate summaries, misinterpreted schemas, and unsupported analytical explanations. These risks stem from structural limitations in LLMs, including noisy training data, next-token prediction objectives, limited reasoning capabilities, ambiguous prompts, and incomplete or inconsistent enterprise datasets (Nakharu & Kumar, 2025; Karne et al., 2025; SnehaGunda, 2025a). This paper synthesizes current academic research and industry best practices into a comprehensive, multi-layered hallucination-mitigation framework tailored for Microsoft Fabric. The framework integrates governance controls, data quality management, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), structured prompting strategies, human-in-the-loop validation, and automated detection and correction mechanisms.

title: The Responsibility Receipt: A Structural Grammar for Accountability in the Age of Delegated Intelligence
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Responsibility Receipt: A Structural Grammar for Accountability in the Age of Delegated Intelligence
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence has made two things cheap at the same time: claims and actions. Documents, credentials, images, testimonials, agreements, payments, screenings, and delegated tasks can now be produced at machine speed. Responsibility records have not kept pace. The result is an assignment gap: a growing class of consequential actions for which responsibility exists in principle but cannot be assigned in practice, because no durable record links the action to a human mandate, a human review, or a human refusal. This article argues that the gap is infrastructural, not primarily moral or legal. It also has a general solution with a specific shape: the responsibility receipt. A responsibility receipt is a bounded, timestamped, tamper-evident, independently verifiable record of the arc of a delegated action. Its seven-stage grammar is Mandate-> Event-> Evidence-> Human Review-> Boundary/Refusal/Correction-> Receipt-> Verification. Drawing on the Roman-canon doctrine of plena probatio, principal-agent theory, and the sociology of audit, I defend three claims. First, the grammar is complete: each stage answers a forensic question that no other stage can answer. Second, it is invariant: the same stages appear across autonomous agents, algorithmic hiring, insurance, informal finance, and care work, while existing instruments such as audit logs, content provenance, verifiable credentials, and statutory record keeping each implement only a subset. Third, the receipt is modest by design. It proves that a bounded record existed at a time and has not been altered; it never proves that the underlying claim is true. That modesty is its strength. As fabrication becomes cheap, verdict infrastructure inherits an arms race it cannot win, while receipt infrastructure gains value because it preserves the one fact later fabrication cannot change: what was witnessed in the past. I state this as the verdict limit: after generative parity, no verdict on artifact authenticity remains adversarially stable by itself. The stable evidence is temporal. The article develops refusal as a first-class accountability object, derives economic implications for insurance, portable trust, human-made process, and machine-to-machine verification, and closes by arguing that the mature institutional forms of the delegated-intelligence economy are waiting for their record technology.

title: The Attention Economy and Digital Dependence: A Structured Critical Review of Cognitive, Psychological, and Social Consequences in the Smartphone Era

detail.title: The Attention Economy and Digital Dependence: A Structured Critical Review of Cognitive, Psychological, and Social Consequences in the Smartphone Era
detail.abstract: Smartphones, social media platforms, streaming services, artificial intelligence systems, and digitally mediated forms of entertainment have become central to everyday life. These technologies provide substantial benefits, including rapid access to information, communication, education, navigation, productivity tools, and social connection. However, their growing role in daily decision-making has also raised concerns about digital dependence, cognitive offloading, attention fragmentation, reduced memory engagement, weakened critical reflection, psychological distress, and changes in social behaviour. This structured critical review examines cognitive, psychological, and social consequences associated with the smartphone-centred attention economy. Particular attention is given to the ways in which engagementoriented platform design, personalized recommendations, notifications, infinite scrolling, short-form video, and algorithmic amplification may influence attention, memory, information evaluation, emotional well-being, and behavioural choices. The reviewed literature does not support the simplistic conclusion that all technology use is inherently harmful. Digital tools can extend cognitive capacity, support learning, reduce routine mental demands, strengthen social communication, and provide access to health and educational resources. Nevertheless, frequent interruptions, compulsive checking, passive consumption, problematic smartphone use, and prolonged exposure to emotionally arousing content may be associated with poorer concentration, sleep disturbance, anxiety, depressive symptoms, misinformation exposure, and reduced self-regulation. The review argues that responsibility for digital well-being should not be placed solely on individual users. Technology companies, educational institutions, researchers, families, health professionals, and policymakers also have roles in developing healthier digital environments. More longitudinal, experimental, culturally diverse, and independently funded research is required to distinguish causal effects from correlations and to identify effective interventions.

title: Towards Optimized Scale Removal in Oilfields: Synergistic Use of,Acoustic Cavitation and Chemical Dissolvers
affiliations: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST), KAUST Research Center, KAUST Research Center, KAUST Research Center, Upstream Advanced Research Center, KAUST Research Center and KAUST

detail.title: Towards Optimized Scale Removal in Oilfields: Synergistic Use of,Acoustic Cavitation and Chemical Dissolvers
detail.abstract: Calcium sulfate (gypsum) scale removal is among the greatest operational issues concerning oil production facilities, as the deposition is detrimental to the equipment and related maintenance results in prolonged downtime. Therefore, investigating process intensification techniques is pivotal for reducing scale removal time. This study focuses on the application of acoustic cavitation to the dissolution of gypsum, demonstrating the efficacy of the technology in improving the rate of the process. With the aid of electron microscopy, this work dives into the cavitation-driven modification of the mechanism of action of two different types of dissolver solutions, potassium carbonate and tetrasodium EDTA. In particular, the dissolution in the first is enhanced 8.5 times, whilst in the second by 55 times due to a modification in the mechanism of action of the converter. The latter dissolves the gypsum layer by layer in ’silent’ conditions (no ultrasound) but shows the formation of deep cavities beyond the superficial layer when ultrasound is applied. The findings enable the utilization of acoustic cavitation as a process intensification tool for scale removal in oil production facilities, paving the way to further studies investigating the field applicability.
